title: Perovskite solar manufacturing could generate $7.92 billion in domestic value addition over 15 years in India - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A new study highlights the potential of perovskite technology to reduce India’s dependence on imported solar manufacturing materials and equipment. It also points to higher energy yields, lower electricity generation costs and opportunities for domestic innovation.
Uma Gupta
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Perovskite solar cells
Perovskite solar technology could generate approximately INR 74,000 crore ($7.92 billion) in domestic value addition in India over the next 15 years, creating opportunities for Indian companies to develop proprietary materials, manufacturing processes and intellectual property (IP), according to a new study by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA) and P3C Technology and Solution.
The study, titled “Perovskite Solar: India’s Atmanirbharta Opportunity in Next Generation PV,” highlights the potential of perovskite technology to reduce import dependence, cut manufacturing costs and foster domestic innovation. It outlines how the technology could help India move beyond conventional crystalline silicon manufacturing and establish a foothold in advanced solar technologies.
India has expanded its domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity and is developing ingot and wafer production facilities under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. However, the country remains heavily dependent on imported polysilicon, wafers and manufacturing equipment.
According to the study, perovskite technology could help address these gaps in India’s solar manufacturing supply chain. Unlike conventional crystalline silicon technology, perovskite solar cell manufacturing can bypass the polysilicon, ingot and wafer production stages, where India’s import dependence is particularly high. This could offer an alternative route to expanding domestic manufacturing while reducing reliance on imported upstream components.
The study also points to potential cost advantages, estimating that capital expenditure for perovskite manufacturing facilities could be 70% to 80% lower than for conventional crystalline silicon production lines.
It further suggests that lower temperature-related performance losses could increase the capacity utilization factor (CUF) from around 20% to 25% and reduce the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) by 30% to 40%. However, these projections remain subject to validation through long-term field performance data.
The study estimates that capex for perovskite solar manufacturing could range from INR 22 ($0.24) to INR 28 per watt, compared with INR 38 to INR 42 per watt for crystalline silicon. It also projects higher energy yields for perovskite modules, with annual generation estimated at 2.19 million units per MW, compared with 1.75 million units per MW for crystalline silicon.
The capacity utilization factor (CUF) could increase from around 20% to 25%, while the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) could fall from INR 2.4–2.7/kWh for crystalline silicon to INR 1.5–1.9/kWh for perovskite, representing a reduction of approximately 30% to 40%. However, the study estimates annual degradation of 0.5% to 1% for perovskite modules, compared with around 0.5% for crystalline silicon.
The study recommends a phased approach to technology adoption, starting with single-junction perovskite solar cells, followed by silicon-perovskite tandem cells based on India’s existing tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) manufacturing infrastructure. This approach could allow domestic manufacturers to leverage existing investments while gradually building capabilities in advanced PV technologies.
To support the transition, the study calls for policy and regulatory measures, including a provisional two-tier classification under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), with clearly defined stability milestones. It also recommends dedicated research and development (R&D) and pilot project funding through the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), alongside independent techno-economic assessments of commercial viability.
“India’s solar manufacturers have made significant investments in backward integration across cells, wafers and ingots. Perovskite is a promising next step that builds on this foundation. ISMA looks forward to working with the Government and industry on an enabling pathway for next-generation solar technologies,” said Amit Manohar, secretary general of ISMA.
“P3C is developing its own absorber chemistry, assembly line and intellectual property in India. Our modules are undergoing reliability testing at NISE, and our priority is to build the field data that makes this technology bankable. We are glad to work with ISMA to take this conversation to manufacturers and policymakers,” said Sooraj Kumar, co-founder and CEO of P3C Technology and Solutions.
The study concludes that establishing a domestic perovskite manufacturing ecosystem will require sustained investment in research, technology validation, industry participation and policy support. Such efforts could help India expand its role beyond solar manufacturing and deployment to the development and ownership of next-generation PV technologies.

title: European solar module prices face additional pressure from surplus stock, cancelled projects - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a chat with
pv magazine
, Bart Wansink, CEO of Netherlands-based Search4Solar, discussed how surplus modules from cancelled projects, high inventory levels and Chinese manufacturing reforms are shaping European solar module prices. He expects prices to stabilise in 2027, although persistent oversupply could delay a sustained recovery.
Emiliano Bellini
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
The European solar industry is entering a new phase after several years of sharp price declines. Manufacturers, distributors and installers are adapting to a market characterised by excess production capacity, intense price competition and changing purchasing behaviour.
“Over the past six months, we have continued to see pressure on module prices, particularly for TOPCon products,” Bart Wansink, CEO of Netherlands-based solar trading platform Search4Solar, told
pv magazine
. “According to the September 2026 European PV Index published by sun.store, average transaction prices reached approximately €0.114 ($0.125)/W for bifacial TOPCon modules and €0.120/W for monofacial TOPCon modules, excluding VAT and delivery costs.”
Wansink said actual transaction prices can vary considerably depending on order volumes, brands, technical specifications, availability and delivery terms.
“At Search4Solar, for example, we are offering selected solar modules at approximately €0.08/W, depending on purchase volumes and commercial conditions,” he said. “This demonstrates how competitively modules can be priced when large volumes and efficient international distribution come together.”
However, Wansink stressed the importance of distinguishing large-volume transactions from standard distributor pricing. Prices negotiated for container-scale orders do not necessarily reflect those paid by installers purchasing smaller quantities for local delivery.
“Price differences between France, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain are often driven more by logistics, local inventories, order quantities and technical requirements than by fundamentally different manufacturing costs,” he said.
Cancelled projects
Another factor influencing European module prices is the availability of equipment originally procured for solar projects that have been postponed, restructured or cancelled.
Wansink pointed to a transaction involving approximately 100 MW of Tier 1 solar modules that Search4Solar is distributing after the large-scale project for which they were originally intended failed to proceed as planned.
“Instead of remaining tied to one project, these modules can be redistributed to multiple customers across different European markets,” he said. “Solar equipment originally intended for one project can re-enter the market, sometimes at prices that are highly competitive compared with new factory orders.”
Such transactions can offer purchasing opportunities but may also create additional price pressure for conventional distribution channels, according to Wansink.
He added that the ability to redistribute large quantities of modules is becoming increasingly important for manufacturers, project developers and investors seeking to manage surplus equipment.
China’s manufacturing reforms
China’s efforts to address excess manufacturing capacity are another important factor shaping the global solar market.
Chinese manufacturers have faced sustained pricing pressure amid intense competition and persistent oversupply. On 1 April 2026, China eliminated value-added tax (VAT) export rebates for certain photovoltaic products, changing the cost structure for exporters.
“This changes the economics of exporting certain solar products and can create additional pressure on manufacturers’ margins,” Wansink said. “However, we should distinguish between increasing production or export costs and the actual selling prices achieved in Europe.”
He noted that higher export costs would not necessarily translate into higher module prices in Europe, particularly while significant manufacturing capacity and inventory remain available.
According to Wansink, Chinese manufacturers are increasingly focused on protecting their margins, although their ability to secure sustainable price increases will depend on market demand.
“We expect manufacturers to negotiate more carefully and become more selective about certain large-volume transactions,” he said. “Nevertheless, existing European inventories and project-related surplus stock can continue to create downward price pressure, even when manufacturers are attempting to increase their selling prices.”
Outlook for 2027
Looking ahead to the next six to 12 months, Wansink expects European module prices to become more stable, with the possibility of moderate increases during 2027.
“However, we do not expect a dramatic or sustained price recovery without a more meaningful reduction in global manufacturing capacity or a stronger increase in demand,” he said.
Wansink identified several factors likely to determine the direction of European module prices, including manufacturing capacity adjustments in China, European inventory levels and the availability of surplus modules from delayed or cancelled projects.
“The market will be shaped by several key factors, including the gradual rationalisation of Chinese manufacturing capacity, which could help bring production and demand into better balance, and European inventory levels, which will continue to influence short-term pricing,” he said. “At the same time, modules released from cancelled or postponed projects may add further competitive pressure, while the pace of European installations, access to project financing and government policy will ultimately determine how quickly existing stock is absorbed.”
He added that pricing trends could vary across module technologies, manufacturers and product formats.
“We do not believe there will necessarily be one uniform European module price trend,” he said.
Distribution strategies under pressure
Wansink expects inventory management, access to financing and international sales networks to play an increasingly important role in determining the competitiveness of European solar distributors.
“Holding the largest inventory is not necessarily a competitive advantage if prices are falling and financing costs are increasing,” he said. “Instead, successful distributors will need strong customer networks, reliable logistics and the ability to identify demand before committing to large purchases.”
Search4Solar is seeking to expand its role in European module distribution by strengthening relationships with manufacturers, distributors, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors, and installers.
“At Search4Solar, we are building an international renewable energy distribution platform connecting manufacturers, distributors, EPC contractors and installers,” Wansink said. “Our ambition is to distribute increasingly large volumes of solar modules across Europe, with a long-term objective of reaching 1 GW of annual module sales.”
The company is expanding its international sales network, targeting larger EPC companies and developing its digital purchasing capabilities.
Wansink believes distributors with strong international customer networks and efficient inventory turnover will be better positioned to compete in an increasingly price-sensitive market.
“The winners in European solar distribution will not necessarily be the companies holding the most stock,” he said. “They will be the companies with the strongest international customer networks, the fastest stock rotation and the ability to distribute large volumes profitably.”
“The market is moving from simply trading solar panels towards managing a European distribution network,” he concluded. “That is where we see the biggest opportunity for Search4Solar.”

title: Why AI data centers need storage beyond conventional backup power - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
As AI workloads introduce sharper power fluctuations, battery storage is moving closer to computing infrastructure. EVE Energy’s AIDC portfolio illustrates how grid-scale systems, high-rate backup cabinets, and rack-level batteries address different operating demands.
EVE Energy
18 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
AI data centers are changing the duty cycle expected of battery energy storage. Alongside conventional requirements for backup capacity and renewable-energy integration, operators must manage rapid load changes associated with high-density computing. A single battery architecture is unlikely to meet every requirement efficiently.
The distinction begins with response time. At the source-grid interface, storage can support renewable integration, demand management, and frequency regulation. Within power-distribution systems, batteries must sustain high output during short interruptions. At server-rack level, even shorter fluctuations require millisecond-scale intervention.
EVE Energy structures its AIDC offering around these three layers. For source-grid applications, its 20-foot, 5 MWh high-power storage system is designed for 1P operation and frequent cycling, with 93.6% system efficiency and an operating range of −40°C to 55°C. Its S5-1P system uses dedicated 315 Ah frequency-regulation cells with 395 Wh/L energy density. EVE reports no lithium plating under specified 1P charge-discharge and 1.22P frequency-regulation tests — demonstrating cell stability under demanding high-rate operation.
For longer-duration applications, the Mr.Giant 3.0 system integrates 6.9 MWh in a standard 20-foot container using 702 Ah cells. Published specifications include a 10,000-cycle system life at 70% state of health and a system temperature difference of no more than 5°C. Actual performance depends on operating conditions.
At the distribution layer, EVE’s 6C/10C backup cabinets target high-power, short-duration loads and compatibility with UPS and high-voltage DC architectures. The 10C configuration delivers a specified 660 kW over five minutes. At rack level, its battery backup unit uses 21700 LFP cylindrical cells, supports 15C–30C discharge rates, and specifies switchover within 2 milliseconds.
Coordinating cell behavior, battery management, power conversion, and operating strategies across these layers affects reliability and total cost of ownership. EVE combines cell development with BMS and system integration, offering operators a unified engineering interface.
The portfolio is being presented at the EVE Energy booth (N717 North Hall) at RE+ 2026, in Las Vegas, where the growing overlap between energy storage and digital infrastructure is becoming a practical design consideration for developers and system integrators.

Markets & Policy
New regulations aim to encourage battery storage integration at existing solar PV plants, improve grid flexibility, and create additional revenue opportunities for renewable energy developers.
Emiliano Bellini
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Utility-scale
A 132 MW PV plant in Taiwan
Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) has introduced a
regulatory framework
designed to promote the integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) with existing solar photovoltaic installations. The initiative reflects Taiwan’s growing emphasis on grid stability, renewable energy optimization, and the development of a more flexible electricity system.
The guidelines, issued on November 6, 2024, establish a competitive bidding and capacity allocation mechanism for eligible solar power facilities seeking to incorporate battery storage.
Under the new framework, existing grid-connected PV plants exceeding 1 MW in size may participate in the bidding process. Eligible developers are required to install battery storage with a minimum energy capacity equivalent to 2.61 MWh for every MW of rated storage power.
The competitive bidding mechanism determines the battery capacity tariff offered to successful applicants, introducing market-based price competition. Projects receiving capacity allocation approval must generally complete battery installation and grid connection within 15 months.
The framework also requires successful participants to release grid connection capacity equivalent to 1.5 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to applicable conditions. This provision could help improve the utilization of Taiwan’s existing grid infrastructure and create opportunities for additional renewable energy integration.
The framework also includes provisions for a daily guaranteed billing quantity linked to 2.61 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to operational requirements and other conditions.
Electricity discharge will be coordinated according to national utility
Taipower
‘s scheduling and dispatch requirements. This approach is intended to shift part of Taiwan’s solar electricity output from midday periods toward times when stored energy can provide greater value to the electricity system.
Taiwan has been pursuing a broader expansion of renewable energy capacity alongside measures to improve market conditions.
In January 2025, the Ministry of Economic Affairs
announced plans to accelerate solar and offshore wind deployment
, targeting an additional 8.2 GW of combined capacity by the end of 2026. However, deployment has progressed more slowly than initially anticipated.
December 2025 forecast by GlobalData
projected that Taiwan’s cumulative solar capacity would reach 31.2 GW by 2035, with the 20 GW milestone now expected in 2029. The government has also
maintained solar feed-in tariffs for 2026
at the levels established in the second half of 2025, aiming to sustain investment and deployment.
Energy storage is also gaining prominence. In October 2025, French battery manufacturer Saft
announced plans to supply 356 MWh of battery storage
for a project in Taichung, bringing its planned installed capacity on the island to 630 MWh by 2026.
The market has also seen earlier examples of storage integration with solar generation, including a
15 MW/15 MWh battery system connected to a 150 MW solar park
in southern Taiwan.

The Asian Development Bank is providing advisory services for five additional solar and battery storage projects, through a programme aiming to attract more than $1 billion in private investment.
Patrick Jowett
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Energy Storage
Residential
Utility-scale
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is expanding its support for solar and battery energy storage projects in Bangladesh through a three-phase programme covering more than 1 GW of planned capacity.
The bank has agreed to provide transaction advisory services for five additional projects, building on its existing support for the 130 MW Sonagazi solar project in the Feni district of southeastern Bangladesh, which ADB says is due to tender next year.
ADB explains its expanded programme is expected to mobilise more than $1 billion in private sector investment.
The agreement will see ADB work with investment authority Invest Bangladesh and the state-owned Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) to assess the suitability of government-owned land for the five additional projects. Details covering the planned capacity of each individual project are yet to be released.
The bank’s advisory services will cover project preparation, technical and financial assessments, market sounding, tender document preparation, and support for competitive bidding and contract awards.
“Bangladesh has an opportunity to build a more secure, sustainable, and investment-ready energy future,” said Qingfeng Zhang, ADB country director for Bangladesh.
He added that the expanded advisory mandate would help establish a scalable market for clean energy investment by strengthening project preparation, competitive procurement and the conditions needed to attract private capital.
Bangladesh has set a target of generating at least 20% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030, increasing to 30% by 2040. The country currently has 1,871 MW of installed renewable energy capacity, including 1,492 MW of solar.
In October, BPDB approved a
442 MW solar project
with eight hours of battery storage, making it the country’s largest PV project under development. The government also recently established a
$123 million fund for rooftop solar and other renewable energy projects

Markets & Policy
The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement on new rules designed to accelerate permitting and grid connections for renewable energy projects across the bloc. EU member states will have 18 months to transpose the directive into national law following its formal adoption.
Emiliano Bellini
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
The EU Parliament
The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement on legislation aimed at streamlining permitting procedures for renewable energy projects and energy infrastructure across the EU.
“With tonight’s provisional agreement on the permitting directive, we have completed the first half of the European grids package. We are delivering on the ambition in the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, energy and the environment.
“Successfully concluding the permitting directive follows months of interinstitutional negotiations, and this agreement represents one of the most significant legislative milestones in the EU’s energy agenda. I am proud of Ireland’s role in concluding this cornerstone file during our presidency,” he added.
The provisional agreement still requires endorsement by the Council and the European Parliament. Following legal review, both institutions will formally adopt the legislation. EU member states will then have 18 months to transpose the directive into national law.
The proposed rules aim to remove administrative barriers, shorten permitting timelines and accelerate grid connections for renewable energy projects, energy storage facilities and electric vehicle charging stations. They also seek to simplify authorization procedures for new electricity and gas infrastructure.
“Member states will be able to prioritize the roll-out of renewable energy and electricity grids by presuming them to be of overriding public interest,” the Council said in a statement. “The provisional agreement aligns with the Council’s position, leaving to member states the discretion not to apply this principle in order to protect security and defence and cultural heritage interests.”
The agreement builds on the
European Grids Package unveiled by the European Commission in December 2025
. The package includes measures to accelerate infrastructure planning, improve grid connection procedures and revise the Trans-European Networks for Energy (TEN-E) Regulation. In September, the European Parliament’s industry committee
backed proposals to streamline cross-border energy infrastructure development
, including changes to planning, permitting and investment procedures.
The latest agreement also comes amid mounting concerns over grid congestion and delays in connecting renewable energy projects across Europe. According to
research published by Aurora Energy Research in January
, more than 1 TW of renewable energy capacity was awaiting grid connection across the continent, with permitting procedures taking up to a decade in some markets. A
subsequent analysis by Ember
identified a gap of approximately 120 GW between planned renewable energy deployment and available grid capacity across most EU member states, highlighting the scale of the infrastructure constraints facing the sector.

content:
Markets & Policy
France’s energy regulator has outlined the terms for a 500 MW technology-neutral renewables tender covering solar, wind and hydropower. The proposed rules introduce an unweighted reference price, raising concerns over market risks, financing costs and limited PV capacity.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
18 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
France’s energy regulator, the Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), has published its opinion on the
draft specifications
for the first round of the
PPE3 Neutre
technology-neutral renewable energy tender, which is expected to launch in January 2027. The tender will allocate just 500 MW of capacity across solar PV, onshore wind, and hydropower projects, while introducing an unweighted market reference price (M0) for the calculation of support payments.
French renewable energy association SER has strongly criticized the limited capacity allocation. Its president, Jules Nyssen, expressed disappointment that the industry’s proposals had not been taken into account, highlighting the gap between the 500 MW available across three technologies and the 1.5 GW of solar capacity initially requested by the association.
The SER has called for dedicated PV tenders covering rooftop, ground-mounted, and hybrid solar-plus-storage installations.
Unweighted reference price increases risks for developers
The draft specifications set a maximum bid price of €100 ($109.6)/MWh. The weighting of the price criterion has also changed significantly compared with previous
PPE2 Neutre
tenders. Previously, price accounted for 70% of the evaluation score, with the remaining 30% allocated to carbon footprint and environmental criteria. Under the new framework, price will account for 95% of the score, intensifying competition among bidders and increasing downward pressure on awarded tariffs.
Beyond the limited capacity allocation, the introduction of an unweighted M0 represents a significant change to the support mechanism. The new benchmark is intended to improve the comparability of bids across technologies and assess how developers account for the risk of electricity price cannibalization. The SER has argued that the mechanism should remain experimental until a more comprehensive review of renewable energy support schemes has been conducted.
The CRE has also identified economic risks associated with the change. Aggregation contracts, which typically run for one to three years, are significantly shorter than the duration of contracts for difference under the premium-based support mechanism. This mismatch exposes producers to greater uncertainty over aggregation costs.
The introduction of an unweighted M0 could therefore lead to higher risk premiums, shorter contract durations, increased financing costs, and a reduction in the proportion of debt that projects can secure.
Battery storage could mitigate market risks
Pairing PV installations with battery energy storage systems could help mitigate these risks by allowing developers to shift electricity exports to periods of higher market prices.
To encourage hybrid projects, the CRE has recommended relaxing some of the eligibility requirements for the first tender round. In particular, developers would not be required to obtain administrative authorization for the storage component before submitting a bid. The regulator also proposed greater flexibility in the conditions for withdrawing storage from a project if the necessary permits cannot be secured or the storage component cannot be financed.
The CRE also welcomed the increase in the minimum eligibility threshold for PV projects from 500 kW to 1 MW.
However, the regulator noted that the lack of visibility over future tender volumes remains a significant constraint for developers. It said this uncertainty should be considered when assessing the results of the first
PPE3 Neutre
tender round.

title: Hybrid monofacial-bifacial PV arrays boost power output under shading - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers tested a nine-module array combining six monofacial and three bifacial panels under 12 illumination patterns. The experiments assessed how module placement and electrical reconfiguration influence power output.
Lior Kahana
18 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Illustration of a PV array combining monofacial and bifacial modules.
A research team in India has experimentally investigated the performance of a photovoltaic array combining monofacial and bifacial solar modules.
“To mitigate power increase and cost, a hybrid PV array arrangement incorporates a small number of bifacial modules within a traditional monofacial array,” the researchers said. “Employing a switching matrix-based reconfiguration approach, the most effective hybrid configuration was dynamically selected.”
The researchers tested different configurations of a 3 × 3 PV array to determine how to increase power output while limiting costs.
They assembled a 3 × 3 PV array with nine modules electrically connected in a total-cross-tied configuration. They first measured the voltage, current, and power output of a reference array comprising nine 10 W monofacial modules. They then replaced three of the modules with 12 W bifacial modules to create a hybrid array.
The team tested six configurations, placing the three bifacial modules in different positions: diagonally in the top-left, center, and bottom-right positions; across the top row; down the leftmost column; in the center and the two bottom corners; in the top-right and two bottom corners; and in the top-middle, top-right, and bottom-right positions. The remaining six positions in each configuration were occupied by monofacial modules.
The researchers conducted rooftop experiments at Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology in southern India under 12 irradiance conditions: no shading, uneven column shading, uneven row shading, diagonal shading, plus-shaped shading, center shading, corner shading, outer shading, short-and-wide shading, long-and-wide shading, left-corner shading, and random shading.
They compared the electrical performance of each hybrid configuration with that of the all-monofacial reference array. They also investigated whether switching between different configurations could improve power output under changing shading conditions.
In the “double-hybrid” analysis, the researchers compared pairs of configurations, while the “triple-hybrid” analysis considered groups of three. For each shading pattern, they selected the configuration delivering the highest power output within each pair or group.
“In the double-hybrid analysis, bifacial placements in the first column and grouped configurations ((2 × 2), (3 × 1), and (3 × 3)) consistently delivered superior performance, with power output ranging from 95 W under no-shading conditions to 26 W under severe shading, outperforming other configurations in nine shading scenarios,” the researchers said. “Similarly, the triple-hybrid comparison showed that first-row and first-column placements, along with grouped configurations, achieved maximum power in a greater number of shading cases.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
An experimental investigation of photovoltaic array with mixed mono-facial and bi-facial modules
,” published in
Scientific Reports
. The research team included scientists from India’s
M. Kumarasamy College of Engineering
Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology
, Sri Vidya College of Engineering & Technology, Vardhaman College of Engineering, and
Chitkara University

title: Austrian company develops 1.2 kW Stirling-based heat and power system to complement solar PV in winter - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Frauscher Motors has integrated a Stirling generator into a wood-pellet heating system to produce electricity during the heating season, when photovoltaic yields are typically lower. The generator can deliver up to 1.2 kW of electrical power, with a reported electrical conversion efficiency of approximately 28%.
Emiliano Bellini
18 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
The Stirling module produces approximately 800 W at a heater-head temperature of 500 C
Austrian engine developer Frauscher Motors has developed a biomass-based combined heat and power (CHP) system that converts heat from a wood-pellet boiler into electricity using a compact Stirling generator.
The company said it has been operating a demonstration system since the end of March 2026 to evaluate heat transfer, automatic cleaning and long-term operating stability.
“We have demonstrated a maintenance-free operating time of 10,000 hours using natural gas as fuel. Long-term tests are ongoing with a view to extending this period,” the company’s CEO, Josef Frauscher, told
pv magazine.
“One of the aims of the biomass research project is to determine the long-term durability of the heat exchanger, which is exposed to the flow of hot flue gas. Our goal is to achieve service lives comparable to those achieved when operating on natural gas,” he added. “Assuming 2,000 hours of operation per heating season and an average utilisation rate of 75% of the rated output, 1.5 MWh can be generated.”
At the center of the installation is Frauscher’s Gen70 Stirling generator, which converts externally supplied heat into mechanical energy and subsequently electricity. The 29 kg unit uses the company’s patented Alphagamma Stirling engine configuration and operates without lubricating oil.
According to measurements conducted in January 2025, the Gen70T delivered 1,201 W of electrical output from approximately 4,256 W of supplied thermal power, corresponding to an electrical efficiency of 28.2%. The test also recorded approximately 2.92 kW of cooling heat output, which can be recovered for heating applications.
The biomass-based combined heat and power (CHP) system
The generator produces approximately 800 W at a heater-head temperature of 500 C and reaches its highest reported efficiency at around 660 C. Frauscher specifies maintenance-free operation for up to 10,000 hours, after which the module can be refurbished by replacing piston rings and roller bearings.
Integration with pellet heating and battery storage
The demonstration system uses a heat exchanger that captures both radiant heat from the glowing pellet bed and convective heat from the combustion gases. According to Frauscher, the configuration allows heat extraction to be adjusted across a wide range of boiler operating conditions.
An automatic cleaning mechanism, activated alongside the burner’s ash-discharge process, removes deposits from heat-transfer surfaces to maintain performance.
The generator starts automatically when sufficient heat flow is available and supplies a charging voltage of 48 V to 53 V DC for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries.
Frauscher’s proposed system architecture includes a 5 kWh LFP battery and a 48 V DC to 230 V AC inverter rated at 3,000 VA. The electricity can be used to supply household loads or charge battery storage, enabling grid-connected, backup or stand-alone operation.
The technology is intended to complement existing residential PV systems by providing electricity during the heating season, when solar generation is typically lower and heating demand increases.
“In 48-volt systems, integration into PV installations takes place directly via the storage battery’s charging connection; in the case of high-voltage batteries, this is achieved via an inverter,” said Frauscher.
Long-term testing underway
Frauscher is continuing to evaluate the durability of thermally stressed components and compliance with flue-gas emission requirements.
The company has not disclosed the installation cost, expected seasonal electricity generation or levelized cost of electricity. These parameters will be important in determining the technology’s economic viability for residential applications.
“There is no other technology that converts thermal energy into electricity in such a simple and therefore cost-effective way,” Frauscher stated. “Consider, for example, complex steam-based processes or high-maintenance wood gasifiers coupled with internal combustion engines. No oil changes are required, and after 10,000 hours of operation, the only wear parts in the mechanical system that need to be replaced are the piston rings and roller bearings.”
Based in St. Marienkirchen near Schärding, Austria, Frauscher Motors has been developing Stirling engine technology for more than two decades. Its generator portfolio covers electrical outputs from approximately 1.2 kW to 7.5 kW.
The company is targeting residential heating systems, off-grid applications and hybrid renewable energy installations, with the aim of providing an additional source of electricity alongside solar PV.

title: South Korean anti-drone radar to protect US refineries, stadiums
content: South Korea’s Hanwha Systems has secured its first radar export contract in the United States, signing a pilot agreement to supply compact, short-range active electronically scanned array (AESA) anti-drone radars to New York-based defense technology firm Rebellion Industries. Deliveries under the initial trial order are scheduled for completion by early 2027, marking a significant step in South Korea’s push to expand defense sensor sales into the world’s largest military and homeland security market.While South Korean defense contractors have previously exported medium- and long-range multifunction air-defense radars to customers across the Middle East and Europe, breaking into the U.S. radar market has long remained a high bar. The agreement builds on Hanwha Systems’ initial entry into the U.S. defense supply chain in December 2025, when it signed a contract with Boeing to supply large-area cockpit displays for F-15 fighter jets.How the compact AESA radar tracks small dronesAnnounced by Hanwha Systems on November 18, 2026, and reported by The Korea Herald, the contract covers a specialized short-range AESA radar engineered specifically to detect and track low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Unlike conventional long-range air-defense radars optimized for high-altitude aircraft and ballistic missiles, this unit focuses on spotting small, slow-moving drones within a detection range of up to 6.2 miles (10 kilometers).To simplify installation across diverse platforms, Hanwha Systems integrated the antenna, main processing unit, and power supply into a single lightweight module. That all-in-one footprint allows the sensor to be mounted on armored vehicles, tanks, and small naval patrol vessels, as well as stationary rooftops and perimeter towers.On the software side, the radar pairs electronically steered beams with an artificial intelligence target-identification algorithm. According to the company, this AI processing helps operators distinguish hostile drones from birds and clutter even when operating through fog, dust, or heavy electromagnetic interference.Under the partnership, Hanwha’s hardware will be integrated with Rebellion Industries’ Sensor OS platform to create an end-to-end counter-drone detection and response suite.Protecting critical US infrastructure firstRather than heading straight to frontline military units, the initial batch of radars supplied to Rebellion Industries is slated for deployment at high-value civilian and industrial sites across the United States. Planned installation locations include oil refineries, corporate data centers, logistics hubs, and sports stadiums, facilities increasingly vulnerable to unauthorized drone incursions and surveillance.Neither company disclosed the financial value of the pilot order or the exact number of units involved, describing the contract as a trial shipment designed to evaluate market performance ahead of negotiations for larger follow-on orders.Expanding production for a broader sensor lineupTo prepare for anticipated demand in both the U.S. and global counter-drone markets, Hanwha Systems plans to introduce automated production lines at its manufacturing plant in Gumi, South Korea, to boost volume capacity and lower unit costs. Alongside the 6.2-mile (10-kilometer) model heading to Rebellion Industries, the company aims to complete development of shorter-range variants, with detection radii of 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) and 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) by early 2027 to offer layered coverage for smaller perimeters and mobile units.

title: New US-made artificial neurons could respond in under 5 nanoseconds
content: Artificial brain cells that fire in under five nanoseconds, targeting AI hardware that consumes up to 500 times less power than today’s systems, could bring brain-inspired computing closer to everyday devices.​Researchers at Oakland University have designed an artificial neuron that combines a tiny magnetic device with a conventional transistor to mimic the way neurons in the human brain communicate. Rather than relying on increasingly complex digital circuits, the design uses the natural behavior of magnetic materials to process information, possibly creating the way for faster and far more energy-efficient AI chips.​With the increased use of artificial intelligence, power demand has become a major challenge for the industry. Large AI models require enormous computing resources, driving up electricity use in data centers and making it difficult to run advanced AI directly on portable or edge devices.​The researchers stated that the human brain remains the benchmark for efficient computing. It performs billions of operations while consuming only about 20 watts of power—roughly the energy needed to run a household light bulb.​By comparison, modern AI systems require dramatically more energy. According to the team, today’s AI inference hardware can consume around 500 times more power than the brain to perform comparable tasks, creating a strong need for new hardware architectures.​Instead of building increasingly larger processors, the researchers looked to biology for inspiration.​”Our goal is to make AI practical on everyday devices instead of depending on massive data centers,” the researchers said, adding that the brain’s efficiency comes from the way its neurons communicate through short electrical pulses rather than continuous computation.​Tiny magnet acts like a neuron​The new artificial neuron consists of a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ), a nanoscale magnetic component paired with a standard transistor commonly found in mainstream electronics.​As current flows through the device, the magnetic element naturally switches states and produces electrical spikes that resemble the firing behavior of biological neurons. Because the device relies on its intrinsic magnetic properties in place of complex digital logic, it requires far fewer circuit components.​The researchers said the neuron responds in less than five nanoseconds, permitting information to be processed at extremely high speeds while keeping energy consumption low.​The study pointed out that, unlike traditional AI chips that repeatedly move data between processors and memory, the magnetic neuron performs computation where the information is stored. This reduces unnecessary data transfers, one of the biggest contributors to AI’s power consumption.Instead of processing information solely as binary signals, the artificial neurons communicate through the timing of electrical spikes, similar to neurons in the brain.The researchers demonstrated this by connecting multiple magnetic neurons into a small neural network. They trained it to solve the exclusive OR (XOR) problem, a widely used benchmark for testing neural networks. The network successfully learned the task by adjusting spike timing instead of relying on conventional digital calculations.​The team said this event-driven approach means the neurons remain largely inactive until new information arrives, helping reduce unnecessary energy use.​Toward low-power AI hardwareIf demonstrated in hardware, the technology could enable energy-efficient AI processors for robots, autonomous systems, smart sensors, wearable electronics, and other edge devices where power is limited.​Because the design combines conventional CMOS transistors with magnetic devices already used in commercial memory technologies, the researchers believe it could integrate more easily with present semiconductor manufacturing processes.​The work is currently based on simulations, and the next step will be to fabricate and experimentally validate the magnetic neurons under real-world operating conditions. If successful, the approach could present a practical path toward AI hardware that is not only faster but also dramatically more energy efficient.​The study was published in IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems.

title: Google backs superhot geothermal tech to fuel 24/7 data center demand
content: Most geothermal plants merely skim the Earth’s upper crust for scalding water. But now a new alliance aims to unlock the extreme heat buried miles below.Google has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Quaise Energy for 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian in Central Oregon. As per a recent announcement, it is slated to begin delivery as early as 2030.This round-the-clock, carbon-free electricity will help run Google’s data center operations in The Dalles. It would also feed into the surrounding regional grid.Vaporizing rock to power data centersTypical geothermal plants are restricted to regions with naturally occurring underground water reservoirs below 600°F. Quaise Energy overcomes this geographic limit with Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) that tap extreme subsurface heat, generating up to 10 times more clean power per well.Originating from MIT nuclear fusion research, Quaise’s millimeter-wave drilling uses a vacuum-tube gyrotron to beam high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole. Rather than grinding rock with steel drill bits that melt under extreme heat, the beam vaporizes rock molecules directly while a purge gas clears out the ash. After drilling over 100 meters through granite in Texas field tests, with more trials underway, the company is now taking a step toward commercial power with Project Obsidian.Project Obsidian will launch in two distinct phases, beginning with conventional drilling rigs to tap superhot geothermal conditions at commercial scale. Following that initial rollout, the site will host the world’s first commercial deployment of millimeter-wave drilling, which retrofits existing rigs to vaporize deep basement rock using high-frequency energy.“We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” said Carlos Araque, CEO and President of Quaise Energy. “Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power.”AI power crunchCompared to weather-dependent solar and wind energy, AI data centers require uninterrupted, round-the-clock power. With geothermal currently supplying only a small part of the world’s electricity, this partnership could transform a niche energy source into a reliable grid staple.For Google, the deal accomplishes two goals: securing reliable electricity for its massive computing infrastructure while shielding local ratepayers from grid strain.Across its three Oregon data center campuses, the tech giant already runs on 83% carbon-free energy and directly funds the grid infrastructure its expansion requires.“Google data centers are long-term investments in the communities we call home,” said Lucia Tian, Head of Advanced Energy Technologies at Google. “This collaboration with Quaise on superhot geothermal will help fuel local economic growth while helping to build a more robust and affordable energy future for Oregon.”Momentum behind Quaise has accelerated rapidly after a $180 million Series B funding round closed in August 2026, including a $35 million stake from drilling giant Nabors Industries.Construction at Project Obsidian is projected to support between 200 and 400 jobs, followed by more than 50 permanent roles in engineering and plant operations.

title: Single-propeller drone sees in every direction without extra sensors
content: Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have developed a single-propeller autonomous drone that uses just one motor to fly and scan its surroundings in all directions.Named PULSAR II, the drone uses continuous body rotation to detect obstacles above, below, and around it with a single LiDAR sensor.The design eliminates the need for multiple sensors or a rotating gimbal while enabling high-speed flight in complex environments such as forests and underground parking lots.The drone has also demonstrated controlled flight during collision tests. “The key is to coordinate the mechanical structure, environmental sensing, and flight control so that this simple design can also handle complex environments,” said Fu Zhang, an associate professor at HKU, in a statement. Single-motor droneThe HKU team has developed a single-propeller autonomous drone that uses its own rotation to scan its surroundings in all directions.PULSAR II runs on a single motor and uses one LiDAR sensor to detect obstacles above, below, and around it. Instead of relying on multiple sensors or a mechanical rotating assembly, it exploits its natural body spin to expand its field of view. The technology could help small drones navigate complex environments such as dense forests, caves, tunnels, and underground facilities, where GPS signals may be unavailable.Conventional quadrotor drones use four motors to control their flight. Expanding their sensing coverage often requires additional cameras, LiDAR sensors, or rotating mechanisms, increasing weight, power consumption, and system complexity. PULSAR II takes a different approach. Its specially designed, swashplate-less propulsion mechanism uses a single motor to drive two propeller blades.The drone uses its natural body spin to combine efficient flight with omnidirectional sensing.Researchers say that by precisely adjusting the motor’s rotational speed during each revolution, the system changes the angle of attack of the blades. This generates the torque needed to control the drone’s flight direction.The drone’s body continuously rotates during flight, allowing a vertically mounted LiDAR sensor to scan its surroundings as the aircraft spins. LiDAR works by emitting laser signals and measuring their reflections to calculate distances to nearby objects. The resulting measurements help build three-dimensional (3D) maps of the environment.In PULSAR II, the combination of body rotation and LiDAR allows the sensor to capture areas that would otherwise remain outside its field of view, including ceilings, floors, and surrounding obstacles.During indoor experiments, the drone initially generated only partial maps before takeoff. Once airborne, its rotating LiDAR collected additional measurements to produce more complete 3D point-cloud maps with fewer blind spots.Operating with a single motor also presents challenges in maintaining precise flight control. The propulsion system does not respond consistently at different rotational speeds, making accurate trajectory tracking difficult. To address this, the researchers developed an experimental propulsion model and a compensation method. They also introduced model predictive control on manifolds to improve flight accuracy.Autonomous forest navigationIn tests, PULSAR II completed high-speed figure-eight trajectories and in-air flipping maneuvers. Its trajectory-tracking error was substantially lower than that of the conventional control method used for comparison.The team also developed a collision-resistant control system and installed a lightweight carbon-fiber protective frame around the drone. During experiments, researchers dropped a soft ball onto the hovering aircraft and arranged for it to collide with and push away obstacles while flying forward. The drone maintained stable flight during these tests.The researchers tested PULSAR II in tree-dense forests and underground parking garages containing pillars, doorways, and overhead pipes. The drone navigated narrow passages and avoided obstacles at speeds exceeding 6 meters per second (20 feet per second).Its onboard system independently handled mapping, obstacle avoidance, path planning, and flight control. The tests did not rely on GPS navigation, external motion-capture equipment, or a ground-based computer. The drone weighs approximately 1.12 kilograms (2.5 pounds) and recorded a measured hovering time of 15 minutes and 50 seconds.The researchers see potential applications in search and rescue, disaster response, and 3D terrain mapping, particularly in environments where satellite navigation signals are weak or unavailable. They plan to improve the drone’s localization capabilities in open environments with insufficient laser-reflecting features.

title: The hypersonic missile threat: Why intercepting such weapons is tough
content:
Difficult for existing radar and missile defense systems
This unpredictable movement makes it difficult for existing radar and missile defense systems to calculate their future position accurately. Furthermore, their ability to fly at relatively lower altitudes than traditional ballistic
missiles
can allow them to remain below the effective detection range of some ground-based radar systems because of the Earth’s curvature.
The extreme temperatures generated by aerodynamic friction can also create technical challenges for onboard sensors, communication systems, and guidance technologies. Additionally, the combination of high speed, maneuvrability, limited warning time, and the need for extremely precise interception makes existing missile defense systems less effective against these
Intercepting hypersonic missiles requires new generation of defense capabilities
Therefore, intercepting hypersonic missiles requires a new generation of integrated missile defense capabilities involving space-based sensors, advanced tracking radars, faster interceptors, artificial intelligence, and improved command-and-control systems. Countries such as the United States, China, and Russia are investing heavily in these technologies to strengthen their defense capabilities. Nevertheless, no missile defense system can currently guarantee the successful interception of every hypersonic missile, making
hypersonic
weapons a significant challenge to modern national and international security.
These missiles can be intercepted through a combination of advanced missile defense systems, space-based surveillance, ground-based radar networks, and high-speed interceptor missiles.
These defense systems aim to detect, track, and destroy an incoming hypersonic missile before it reaches its intended target. The interception process begins with early detection through satellites equipped with infrared sensors, which identify the heat generated by a missile during its flight. Ground-based and sea-based radar systems then attempt to track its movement and predict its trajectory.
Once the missile is detected and tracked, interceptor missiles can be launched to destroy it through direct collision or other interception mechanisms. Advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, integrated sensor networks, and directed-energy weapons are also being researched to improve detection, tracking, and interception capabilities. However, successfully intercepting a hypersonic missile remains a major technological challenge.

title: World’s brightest light source probes nuclear materials live
content: Scientists at the Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) have turned to the world’s brightest light source, the Advanced Photon Source (APS), to probe nuclear materials in real time. This will advance nuclear forensics and improve future nuclear energy production.Nuclear forensics is a critical component of global security, nuclear law enforcement, and non-proliferation efforts. Researchers can determine the origin, manufacturing, and intended use of nuclear materials through scientific examination.Different processing steps leave unique chemical signatures on radioactive material. Studying these signatures could help determine if radioactive material is being diverted from legitimate uses to unauthorized ones.However, these reactions happen so fast that studying them is extremely difficult. This is where the ANL team turned to APS, which is also an Argonne facility. What can APS do? The APS is the world’s brightest X-ray light source. It uses a synchrotron to achieve this, where particles are accelerated in a circular path to generate intense beams. This allows researchers to study the tiniest details in materials. While nuclear forensics has relied on chemical signatures observed after the reactions are complete, the APS allows for these reactions to be studied in real time. Conditions such as temperature, pressure, and the surrounding environment impact the reaction. Using the APS, researchers can observe how the reactions are occurring, the movement of the particles, and the changes occurring in them, all in real time. But to do so, the team had to build customized sample containment boxes where they could carry out the measurements. How did they do it? Since APS is used for a wide range of research activities, working with radioactive materials requires special arrangements. The research team had to work with a limited quantity of nuclear material but also also ensure that it remained in multi-layer, leak-proof containers. To make their measurements, the team designed two containment boxes: one that acts as a heated cell and the other as a flow cell. The heated cell is designed to let researchers expose the nuclear material to different gases and at different temperatures. The flow cell is designed to handle liquid samples and carries out precipitation reactions, i.e., when two liquids react and form a solid product. To establish the standard operating procedures (SOPs) with these new boxes and ensure that they can deliver accurate measurements, the team used nonradioactive materials in their tests. Later, they switched to radioactive materials for the next phase of their research. “We successfully performed plutonium precipitation at the APS using our ​‘lab-in-a-box’ containment system,” said Matthew Swindall, a postdoctoral fellow at ANL working on nuclear forensics software development. ​“We hope that this new capability will open up a whole range of research in nuclear forensics and fuel cycle technologies.”The boxes were made using 3D-printed parts with easily available materials, thereby making them cost-effective. They can further be adapted for applications beyond nuclear forensics. “Our results aligned with already existing data. It makes me feel confident that the apparatus we built is doing what we want it to do,” said Anna Servis, principal radiochemist at ANL, in a press release.

title: US tests 180-mile Chunmoo missile offshore for future Navy strikes
content: Hanwha Defense USA has demonstrated a new way to deploy precision-guided missiles at sea, launching its Chunmoo rocket system from a vessel off Mississippi’s coast. The November 15 test used a palletized launcher aboard a missile test range vessel operated by The Spaceport Company (TSC).The demonstration brings land-based rocket artillery technology closer to maritime operations. It also explores how the U.S. Navy could deploy long-range strike weapons from different types of vessels. Hanwha conducted two Chunmoo missile launches as part of the testing campaign.Testing maritime missile capabilitiesHanwha designed the demonstration to evaluate how its Multiple Fixed-Launch Module (MFOM) platform operates in a maritime environment. The palletizable configuration allows operators to move the launcher between platforms without relying on permanently installed weapon systems.That flexibility could prove useful for naval operations involving smaller vessels. It could also expand weapon deployment options across crewed and uncrewed ships.The test focused on validating the launcher and its electronic systems during offshore operations. Engineers also collected technical data to assess the platform’s performance. Those findings will help guide further development of maritime precision-strike capabilities.Hanwha Defense USA Executive Vice President for Missiles Kevin Schoonover said the company wants to address the U.S. Navy’s demand for modern maritime strike systems.He described the combination of Chunmoo missiles and palletized launchers as a potentially lower-cost option. Schoonover also pointed to the platform’s compatibility with next-generation crewed and uncrewed vessels.Data from the demonstration could inform future distributed maritime operations. It may also help shape expeditionary strike systems using palletized and containerized launcher configurations.Offshore testing infrastructureThe Spaceport Company provided the vessel and offshore launch infrastructure for the demonstration. The Mississippi-based provider specializes in mobile launch platforms for commercial spaceflight and national security missions.Its operations include launches from ships, barges and semi-submersible offshore platforms. TSC says it has supported more than 10 launches using its mobile infrastructure.Magnet Defense also participated in the exercise. The Hanwha partner monitored and evaluated the missile launch using its Magnet Research Vessel.The involvement of both companies adds another dimension to the demonstration. Offshore missile testing requires more than a functioning launcher. Range infrastructure and tracking capabilities also play important roles in collecting reliable performance data.Hanwha expands naval ambitionsHanwha’s maritime testing program aims to establish a repeatable process for demonstrating sea-based missile launches. The company plans to use the results to refine future maritime weapons configurations.Its work with Magnet Defense also extends beyond missile testing. The companies announced a strategic partnership in April to develop medium unmanned surface vessels (MUSVs) for the U.S. Department of War.Such vessels could eventually offer additional platforms for distributed naval operations. Pairing unmanned surface vessels with modular weapon systems could give military planners more deployment flexibility. As of now, the Mississippi demonstration represents a test milestone, not confirmation of an operational Navy deployment. Further testing and evaluation will determine how the Chunmoo system performs in maritime environments.

title: Boston Dynamics Atlas humanoid set for first semiconductor factory tests in 2027
content: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robot is set to enter semiconductor manufacturing for the first time, with GlobalFoundries (GF) preparing to test the machine at its facilities from early 2027.The chipmaker will become the first semiconductor manufacturer to join Boston Dynamics’ Atlas early adopter program, as the two companies expand a robotics partnership that has already brought the company’s four-legged Spot robots into factory operations.The agreement also expands Spot deployments across GF’s manufacturing network in Malta, New York; Burlington, Vermont; Dresden, Germany; and Singapore. The robots will support autonomous inspections and asset management at the semiconductor facilities.The Atlas program will initially focus on evaluating potential humanoid applications, assessing integration requirements and preparing the facilities for the technology. The companies also plan to conduct early testing and training for specific tasks.They have not disclosed which tasks Atlas will perform or how many robots will take part in the program.Spot completes 90,000 inspectionsWhile Atlas remains in the testing stage, Spot has already delivered measurable results at GF’s facilities.The companies have worked together for more than four years, with Spot first deployed at the chipmaker’s Burlington site. The program was later expanded to Singapore, where two robots have traveled nearly 900 kilometers through sub-fab areas since April.During that period, they completed more than 90,000 inspections with a reported mission success rate of 99 percent.GF also redeployed 875 routine inspections in just two weeks using updated hardware and software. The company plans to more than double that workload using Spot’s advanced visual inspection capabilities.The inspections collect data from thousands of monitoring points, helping GF move from reactive maintenance towards predictive maintenance.“Spot has helped us shift from reactive to predictive maintenance, collecting data across thousands of inspection points to prevent downtime and keep our fabs running more efficiently,” said Pradip Singh, chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries.Atlas explores factory tasksThe upcoming Atlas program will assess how humanoid robots could support semiconductor manufacturing operations. Its early adopter workshop will examine potential use cases, customer readiness and the integration requirements for introducing humanoid machines into industrial facilities.The initiative will also include early testing and training for specific task execution. It will complement GF’s wider effort to develop employees’ skills in AI and automation.For Boston Dynamics, the partnership extends Atlas testing beyond the automotive sector, where the company has been developing applications for the humanoid platform.“GlobalFoundries was one of our earliest customers to adopt Spot, and we are excited to see the program continue scaling across the globe,” said Zack Jackowski, chief product and technology officer at Boston Dynamics.The company said the data collected through existing robot deployments could also support future manufacturing innovation.The expanded collaboration reflects growing interest in using mobile and humanoid robots to inspect industrial environments, collect operational data and explore tasks that could eventually be automated. However, the Atlas program at GlobalFoundries remains an early-stage evaluation rather than a confirmed rollout for routine factory work.

title: Tesla unveils world's most advanced solid-state power platform
content: Tesla has unveiled a new power electronics platform that could change how large energy projects connect to the electrical grid. Called Powercore, the system combines several power conversion functions into a single medium-voltage unit. It targets growing electricity demands from data centers, battery storage facilities, and utility-scale solar installations.The platform aims to reduce conversion losses while simplifying electrical infrastructure. Tesla plans to manufacture Powercore in the United States, with its first units expected to enter operation in 2027.A new approach to power conversionPowercore combines the functions of a transformer, inverter, and circuit breaker inside one enclosure. It converts electricity between medium-voltage alternating current (AC) and low-voltage direct current (DC). Conventional installations typically require separate equipment to handle these tasks.Tesla claims the platform achieves peak efficiency of 98.86 percent. It can deliver up to 9 megavolt-amperes (MVA), equivalent to 7.4 megawatts continuously. Its grid-forming configuration can also reach 10 MVA.Introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf— Tesla Megapack (@Tesla_Megapack) November 17, 2026The system supports AC voltages between 10 and 34.5 kilovolts. Its DC operating range extends from 800 to 2,000 volts. Tesla has also integrated a solid-state circuit breaker that reportedly clears electrical faults up to 1,000 times faster than conventional breakers.Faster fault clearing can limit electrical damage and improve equipment protection. Powercore also eliminates the flammable insulating oil used in conventional transformers. Its modular design allows technicians to service individual components without replacing the entire unit. Tesla plans to offer warranties of up to 25 years. The company also promises system availability guarantees of at least 99.9 percent.Targeting next-generation data centersData centers represent one of the platform’s biggest potential applications. Their growing computing demands require increasingly complex power infrastructure. Most facilities currently receive electricity at 415 to 480 volts AC before converting it for different systems.The industry is moving toward 800-volt DC architectures. Powercore can convert medium-voltage electricity directly into 800-volt DC. That eliminates intermediate conversion stages and could reduce the equipment needed inside large facilities.Tesla says lower conversion losses could allow operators to run more GPUs using the same available grid connection. Built-in redundancy also gives Powercore a claimed product-level availability of up to 99.7 percent.Tesla is working with Nvidia on engineering efforts to support 800-volt DC power architectures in future data centers. Megapack battery systems can also connect directly to the DC bus. They provide backup power and help manage fluctuations in electricity demand.Bringing solar and storage togetherPowercore also addresses challenges facing utility-scale solar developers. Transformer supply shortages can delay new installations, while inverter failures contribute to lost generation. Tesla’s platform converts electricity from solar arrays directly into medium-voltage AC.It supports existing 1,500-volt DC solar installations and emerging 2,000-volt systems. Its modular design also allows technicians to service components without replacing entire units.Battery storage projects could benefit from a similar change. Conventional Megapack installations use two conversion stages to move electricity between batteries and the grid. Powercore reduces that process to a single stage, potentially improving efficiency and energy output.Tesla estimates that a 100-megawatt data center could run on 500 megawatts of solar capacity paired with 1.7 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. The configuration would allow the facility to draw power from solar and storage systems through an 800-volt DC architecture.Powercore will be manufactured in the United States, although Tesla has not provided a specific production start date. The company currently reports 140 GWh of annual Megapack manufacturing capacity. Of that total, 90 GWh comes from facilities across California, Texas, and Nevada.

title: New Texas 60MW data center targets zero water use for cooling
content: Giga Energy has announced a $1 billion lease agreement with an undisclosed US-based AI cloud provider to develop a 60-megawatt (MW) data center campus in Hunt County, Texas. The facility will use a closed-loop cooling system that operates without municipal or groundwater for computing operations.Called Project Clay, the approximately 30-acre development is being built by Giga Energy, which will develop, own and operate the campus. The company broke ground in July and expects the facility to be ready for service in spring 2027.The project is designed to address growing concerns about the environmental and infrastructure demands of large-scale computing facilities. As demand for AI processing capacity rises, data center developers face increasing scrutiny over their electricity requirements, water consumption and impact on surrounding communities.Giga Energy says its new GigaBase system combines modular construction with dedicated electrical infrastructure and water-efficient cooling to reduce the burden on local resources.Closed-loop cooling cuts water demandUnlike conventional data center cooling systems that can rely on evaporative cooling, Project Clay will use a fully closed-loop system to cool its computing equipment. Giga Energy said the system operates independently of municipal and groundwater supplies.The only water consumption at the facility will be for employee facilities, including sinks and bathrooms. The company estimates this usage will be comparable to that of two homes annually.The development will also use dedicated electrical infrastructure that taps underutilized capacity in the county. Giga Energy said the arrangement is designed to prevent the facility from drawing on distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses.Water and electricity consumption have become major considerations in data center development, particularly in regions facing resource constraints. Large computing facilities require substantial power to operate servers and cooling equipment, placing additional demands on local infrastructure.Giga Energy said Project Clay was designed to address these concerns while bringing new computing capacity to the region.Modular design speeds constructionThe company is using a factory-first construction approach for the project, manufacturing much of the facility off-site before assembling it at the Hunt County location. Giga Energy said this approach could reduce construction time to under eight months, less than half the time required for traditional builds.The modular approach is also expected to reduce truck traffic, road disruption and construction activity around nearby communities. The company said the GigaBase system is intended to make data center deployment faster while reducing pressure on local infrastructure.Project Clay is expected to create approximately 300 construction jobs during development and 24 permanent full-time positions. Giga Energy estimates annual salaries for the permanent roles will range from $116,000 to $180,000.The company also expects the campus to generate millions of dollars in recurring annual tax revenue for Hunt County. These funds could support local schools, public infrastructure, emergency services and other public needs, although Giga Energy has not disclosed a specific revenue estimate.The $1 billion lease agreement marks a major commitment to the facility, although the identity of the cloud provider has not been disclosed.As AI computing demand continues to expand, projects such as Project Clay highlight how developers are exploring modular construction, dedicated power infrastructure and closed-loop cooling to address the resource demands of data centers.

title: Microsoft takes on Claude with coding models costing 95% less
content: Microsoft has unveiled seven new models under its MAI family, targeting coding, cybersecurity, image editing, speech, transcription and automated decision-making as it looks to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic on performance and cost.Announced on November 17 at its Ignite conference, the lineup includes MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Code 2 Flash, MAI Image 2.7, MAI Realtime 1, Dragon Copilot Transcribe and Decision 1.1.The launch reflects Microsoft’s push to make advanced models more affordable for businesses running automated agents continuously. The company said rising token costs are making price-performance increasingly important for enterprises looking to scale these systems.Microsoft is positioning the models for specific workloads rather than relying on a single system for every task. It also highlighted Maia 200, its second-generation AI accelerator, which is running its largest models in production.Microsoft targets lower costsMAI Cyber 2 Flash is designed for continuous cybersecurity monitoring and defensive work, including identifying and patching vulnerabilities in live production systems. Microsoft claims it matches GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGymE2E benchmark.The company said the model builds on earlier MAI Cyber systems used by defenders. Its predecessor accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, Microsoft’s security assessment platform, while 90% of scans that began with MAI continued using it.For software developers, MAI Code 2 targets everyday enterprise coding tasks. Microsoft said it delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s coding performance at about 40% of the price. Against Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, it claims 96% of the performance at just 5% of the cost.A lighter version, MAI Code 2 Flash, is aimed at routine tasks such as code explanations, targeted edits and fixes. It is available in GitHub Copilot and in limited preview through Microsoft Foundry.Models span image and speechMicrosoft also introduced MAI Image 2.7, which it says ranks first in image editing on Artificial Analysis. The company claims it outperforms OpenAI’s GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst at one-fifth of the price. Its text-to-image generation performance ranks fourth on the same evaluation.MAI Realtime 1 is Microsoft’s first speech-to-speech model, built for natural conversations with low latency. It starts at $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe, meanwhile, is based on MAI Transcribe 2 and powers 10 million patient encounters each month, according to Microsoft. The company said it has halved multilingual transcription error rates.Decision 1.1 provides model routing within applications, directing tasks to larger models only when needed. Microsoft said it is 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT-Sol 6.1 and is used by 4,000 customers.The company is also introducing MAI Licensed Weights, allowing businesses to customise models with proprietary data and run them in their own Azure environments.Alongside the models, Microsoft highlighted Maia 200, its second-generation accelerator for AI workloads. The chip is in production, running Microsoft’s largest models and delivering up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt than leading GPU infrastructure, according to the company.By combining specialised models, customisable weights and in-house accelerators, Microsoft aims to give businesses more control over how they deploy and pay for automated systems. The announcement comes as major technology companies compete to lower the cost of running increasingly capable models.
