title: Apple, NSA and Gmail disruptions put US tech systems under strain
content: A series of technology disruptions has affected major U.S. companies and government agencies, raising questions about the reliability of critical digital infrastructure. Apple began restoring several consumer services after an internal software update triggered widespread problems on Tuesday, November 17. Separately, the National Security Agency (NSA) reported intermittent problems with its classified communications network. Gmail also faced a surge in user complaints, although Google denied evidence of a widespread service disruption.The incidents have affected different parts of the technology landscape, from consumer authentication systems to intelligence communications. They also follow recent disruptions involving Microsoft Outlook, U.S. banking services and aviation infrastructure. Apple recovers from outageApple experienced widespread service disruptions on Tuesday, affecting customers across several regions. Users reported difficulties accessing Apple Accounts, downloading applications, and using various iCloud services. Apple Pay, Apple Music, and device activation also appeared among the affected services.The problems prevented some customers from completing routine tasks. Users encountered authentication failures, connection errors, and repeated password verification prompts. People setting up new iPhones or restoring existing devices also reported activation difficulties.Apple confirmed several incidents through its official System Status portal. The company later told USA TODAY that an internal software update triggered the disruption. It also told Bloomberg that a cyberattack did not cause the incident.“We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” Apple said. The company also confirmed that several popular services had recovered.The incident offers an interesting look at how Apple’s interconnected infrastructure supports everyday device operations. Account authentication connects users to services that handle software downloads, cloud storage and digital purchases. Problems within those systems can therefore affect seemingly unrelated features.NSA faces network problemsApple’s recovery coincided with a separate disruption inside one of America’s most sensitive intelligence agencies. The NSA experienced intermittent problems with NSA Net, its classified internal communications network.A person familiar with the matter described the disruption to Fox News Digital. The source said critical communications capabilities remained operational despite the technical difficulties.Agency officials also introduced staggered arrival times for personnel. The arrangement prevents tens of thousands of employees from attempting simultaneous computer logins. Officials hope this approach will reduce pressure on systems during recovery efforts.The precise cause remains unclear. However, the agency reportedly has several backup facilities available to maintain essential operations.NSA Net handles classified communications among agency personnel. Any interruption raises questions about operational resilience, particularly when employees depend on secure digital systems.Gmail reports raise questionsGoogle also faced scrutiny after Downdetector recorded more than 2,800 Gmail complaints by noon Eastern Time on Tuesday. Most reports involved missing incoming messages, although some users described access problems. Google disputed suggestions of a broader service disruption.We want to be clear that we aren’t currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption, and you can always check real-time status on our Status Dashboard: https://t.co/hXJj1ijxrA— News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle) November 17, 2026Google’s response does not establish that every reported problem was unfounded. Individual users or smaller groups could still have experienced genuine delivery difficulties.Recent disruptions involving Microsoft Outlook, banking platforms, and FAA systems have added pressure to America’s technology infrastructure. The FAA temporarily halted flights nationwide following a telecommunications failure. Major banks also experienced reported service interruptions.

title: How hackers used an Optimizely flaw to target data and crypto
content: Optimizely confirmed on November 17 that attackers had exploited a vulnerability in its website experimentation platform to inject malicious code into customer projects associated with 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, Zoom, HSBC and Salesforce.The disclosure followed an investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI, which identified 188 infected scripts after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malicious activity was first detected on November 16 and exposed website visitors to potential payment-card theft, cryptocurrency fraud, and attacks targeting Apple devices.Attackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Experimentation platform to gain unauthorized access and inject JavaScript into customer projects. The compromised scripts were subsequently delivered to visitors through websites using the platform’s tools for testing and personalization.Shared software creates risksThe findings highlight how vulnerabilities in widely used third-party software can expose multiple organizations without attackers having to infiltrate each company’s internal network.Optimizely provides tools that businesses use to test different webpage designs, compare content and personalize visitor experiences. Its software is integrated into customer websites, creating a shared route through which malicious code can reach visitors.Report URI identified infected scripts associated with 178 organizations. However, this does not mean attackers independently breached all 178 companies or accessed their internal networks.The affected websites included those associated with GitLab, IKEA, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, alongside major media and technology companies.Financial organizations represented the largest category in the findings, accounting for 32 organizations. However, the incident does not establish a widespread compromise of US banking systems or payment networks.The injected JavaScript was designed to capture payment-card details entered into websites’ own forms, replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled ones, and collect certain browser cookies and screenshots.Researchers also documented approximately $7,000 in cryptocurrency received by attacker-controlled wallets during the incident. However, they could not establish how much of this was directly linked to visitors of affected websites.Optimizely addresses security breachReport URI also identified two iOS exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, delivered through the malicious scripts to visitors using Apple devices. However, researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised.Visitors who entered payment information on affected websites should monitor their card statements for suspicious transactions. Cryptocurrency users should verify wallet addresses before confirming transfers and install the latest available security updates on their devices.Optimizely said it blocked the vulnerability, removed injected code from affected customer projects, and took steps to secure impacted accounts. The company also ended active sessions, revoked authentication tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and introduced additional safeguards against unauthorized code delivery.Report URI documented a rapid cleanup of infected scripts. By 9:52 p.m. UTC on November 16, only one of the 188 initially identified scripts remained infected. All identified infected files were subsequently cleaned.The incident highlights the risks of relying on shared website components, where a single vulnerability can expose visitors across numerous organizations without necessarily compromising the companies’ internal networks.

title: Radar firm opens US plant after deploying 150,000 sensors worldwide
content: A radar manufacturer has just launched a new factory in the US that is capable of producing 44,000 radar sensors for drones, autonomous vehicles (AVs), as well as other advanced technologies, annually. Located in Lenexa, Kansas, the facility was opened by Ainstein, a radar sensor firm founded in 2015. It is expected to increase the US’ domestic production capacity and meet the growing global demand for advanced radar technology.Zongbo Wang, PhD, Ainstein’s founder and CEO, stated that the company’s radar sensors are already in use in over 40 countries. The firm has reportedly deployed more than 150,000 units globally.He highlighted that the sensors support the safety and autonomous operations of unmanned aircraft, construction vehicles, agricultural equipment, and commercial fleets. The plant officially began operations on November 13. The ribbon-cutting ceremony was attended by employees, business leaders, partners, and community representatives.Meeting growing demandsThe factory is part of the firm’s wider efforts to produce more radar sensors and improve its supply chain. The demand for reliable radar sensors continues to rise. Estimates suggest that the radar sensor market will surge to USD 56.3 million by 2034. The Lenexa plant will tackle these needs by adding capacity to manufacture 44,000 radar sensors each year. Ainstein stated that radar sensors use radio waves to detect objects and measure their distance, speed, and movement. They can work in darkness and challenging weather conditions. Unmanned aircraft can use radar to detect obstacles, while agricultural and construction vehicles can rely on the technology to monitor their surroundings.Ainstein celebrates the Lenexa facility grand opening. Credit: AinsteinThe company also supplies radar technology for aerospace, professional sports, specialty vehicles, and emerging technologies. Wang highlighted the company’s growth since its establishment in Kansas over a decade ago. “We started Ainstein in Lawrence eleven years ago with a small team of engineers and a conviction about what radar could do,” he said. “Today our radars support autonomy in the air and on the ground in over 40 countries.”A bigger US radar supplyThe company hopes to increase the domestic production of radar sensors used in essential systems. Ainstein stressed that unmanned aircraft programs increasingly require locally produced sensors in large quantities. The new factory will provide additional capacity to meet these requirements.It will also give the company more flexibility to support customers as they expand their vehicle fleets and autonomous operations. Ainstein said the facility is only the first step in its long-term plans to expand production capacity.Ainstein’s radar sensors displayed at the Kansas facility. Credit: AinsteinThe company expects its investment in domestic manufacturing to support future growth as radar technology becomes increasingly important across commercial and industrial applications.“This facility is the next chapter in Ainstein’s growth strategy,” Wang concluded in a press release. “It allows us to continue expanding our production to meet rising global demand and the long-term commitments we have made to our customers, and we are proud to be doing that in Kansas, where it all started.”Ainstein develops radar sensors for manufacturers, government contractors, and technology companies. it is backed by Doosan Bobcat, a North Dakota producer of farm and construction equipment.

title: Jensen Huang breaks his silence on a possible Nvidia CEO comeback
content: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has signaled that he remains open to reclaiming the company’s top position. His first public statement since leaving the chipmaker places the decision squarely in the hands of its board. Huang says he would welcome a return if directors believe his leadership would benefit Nvidia and its stakeholders.The statement arrived Tuesday, November 17, following days of speculation about his future. Huang stepped down on November 12, ending a 33-year run at the company he co-founded in 1993. His departure followed revelations about extramarital relationships and growing scrutiny surrounding his personal and professional conduct.Huang acknowledges his mistakesIn his statement, Huang acknowledged that his personal decisions had created serious difficulties for Nvidia’s leadership. He also accepted responsibility and pledged to cooperate with an independent investigation.“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote.He added that he regretted creating problems for the board. The former CEO also thanked colleagues, investors, business partners and customers who had contacted him following his departure.Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026Huang said he had received considerable encouragement to resume leadership as Nvidia navigates complicated market conditions. He specifically referenced the company’s competitive position and growing geopolitical challenges.“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he stated.His willingness to return does not necessarily mean Nvidia’s directors will reconsider their decision. Reports indicate that the board currently has no plans to reinstate him. CFO Colette Kress continues to serve as interim CEO while directors search for a permanent successor.Investigation clouds potential returnHuang’s resignation followed reports about relationships with multiple women, including an Nvidia executive. One relationship involved Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.U.S. intelligence officials have reportedly raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged connections to Chinese intelligence. Those claims have attracted particular attention because Nvidia’s advanced processors sit at the center of Washington’s technology competition with Beijing.The controversy also raises questions about Nvidia’s business relationships and potential national security implications. The board has launched an independent investigation into the matter, which Huang says he will support.Political scrutiny could complicate any potential comeback. Huang is expected to testify before congressional committees on December 1. Lawmakers intend to question him about his relationships and Nvidia’s business dealings involving China-linked companies.Support for his reinstatement has nevertheless gained traction across the technology industry. An online petition calling for his return has collected more than 180,000 signatures. Several prominent technology figures and investors have also expressed support.Investor Brad Gerstner initially suggested that Nvidia consider bringing Huang back. However, he later clarified his position during a Semafor event on Monday. Gerstner argued that the investigation should proceed before anyone reaches a conclusion.He also questioned whether Huang had fully informed the board about his conduct. Gerstner stressed that corporate leadership cannot place anyone above accountability.Nvidia now faces a leadership transition during a particularly important period for the semiconductor industry. Huang’s influence helped establish the company as a dominant supplier of processors for artificial intelligence infrastructure. Whether that legacy will translate into another opportunity at the helm remains uncertain.

title: Ghost radar detects enemy drones with ordinary TV and radio signals
content: A UK defense company has developed a new cheap radar that can detect drones and track hostile aircraft from an SUV without revealing its location to the enemy. Dubbed a “ghost radar,” the novel technology was developed by BAE Systems, a London-based multinational aerospace, arms and information security company. It uses existing TV broadcasts, radio transmissions and mobile networks in order to monitor the skies rather than emitting its own signals.According to BAE Systems, the new passive radar costs up to 10 times less than many existing systems. It is also compact and can be deployed from SUVs. This makes it suitable for both military operations and urban environments.The system can detect targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft. It also provides detailed data about their speed, direction, distance and altitude. “It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected,” Chris Shepherd, BAE Systems’ Digital Intelligence & Land business Product Manager for CUxS, said. A hidden radarA radar (radio detection and ranging) system uses radio waves to determine the distance and velocity of the targets they strike. It is made up of a transmitter to send out radio signal and a receiver to catch reflected energy from the targets. Although this makes it possible to detect aircraft and other threats, the emitted signals can also reveal the radar’s position to enemies. To address this challenge, BAE Systems’ passive radar relies on existing sources, among which digital TV broadcasts and mobile networks.The cost-effective covert radar technology.Credit: BAE Systems / Richard BrownAs per the company, the system analyzes how these signals interact with objects in the air. It then detects and tracks potential threats without actually revealing its own location through radar emissions. “While people are sat at home watching TV, our new radar technology can use transmissions from TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks,” Shepherd explained. More than military useWhile initially designed for military use, the new radar could also be deployed to protect civilian infrastructure. BAE Systems identified airports, power stations and other critical sites as potential applications, particularly where conventional radar emissions may be restricted.On top of that, because the system does not transmit its own radar signals, it can run without adding to existing electromagnetic activity. Its portable design could also make it easier to deploy in urban areas.Members of the BAE Systems team behind the new passive radar technology.Credit: BAE Systems / Richard BrownShepherd is certain that the radar system could be valuable for law enforcement agencies, military personnel, as well as operators of critical national infrastructure. “We’re harnessing the signals that all of us use already in our day to day lives to give police and armed forces the ability to protect us far more cheaply and safely than current passive radar systems,” he concluded in a press release.BAE Systems noted the technology is up to 10 times cheaper than existing passive radar systems. It will now undergo real-world tests, such as live trials with defense, law enforcement and critical infrastructure partners throughout 2027.

title: New lithium find could boost North America’s race to beat China
content: North America’s race to secure domestic battery metals gained fresh momentum in Northwestern Ontario. Rock Tech Lithium has found a potentially large new lithium-bearing deposit at its Victory Project in Northwestern Ontario. The firm uncovered a major spodumene-bearing pegmatite at this site. Interestingly, it has doubled the size of the area where it is actively searching for the battery metal from six kilometers to 16 kilometers (roughly 3 miles to 9 miles).The 150-by-60-meter (492 feet by 196 feet) surface exposure tested positive for lithium using handheld tools. However, these initial findings do not yet confirm consistent underground lithium grades, true deposit thickness, or historical data at Last Resort.“From the outset, Victory offered an exciting combination of scale potential at Bounty and encouraging historical grades at Last Resort,” said Mirco Wojnarowicz, CEO of Rock Tech. “The new discovery adds another important piece to the geological picture and a significant new dimension to our exploration potential. We are only beginning to understand what Victory may have to offer – and we are excited about what lies ahead.”Aerial view of the new discovery, showing a surface exposure approximately 60 metres wide and 150 metres along strike, Source: Rock Tech Lithium.Third major lithium zoneAustralia, China, and Chile supply roughly three-quarters of the world’s raw lithium. Batteries for electric vehicles, grid storage, and personal electronics consume nearly 90 percent of that global output, while smaller shares go toward ceramics, glass, industrial greases, air treatment, and medicine.Spodumene-bearing deposits, known geologically as lithium-cesium-tantalum (LCT) pegmatites, are hard-rock formations that supply most of the world’s mined lithium. These coarse-grained rocks hold large, lithium-rich crystals that companies can extract through conventional mining and refine into battery-grade chemicals faster than salty brine sources.Rock Tech secured an option in June 2026 to fully acquire the 9,875-hectare (about 24,400 acres) Victory exploration property, which sits roughly 45 kilometers ( over 27 miles) east of Kenora, Ontario.Prospectors Jason LeBlanc and Jace Angell spotted the outcrop roughly 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) east of the existing Bounty Pegmatite during a field program launched in late October. The surface exposure measures about 150 meters along strike and at least 60 meters across, with visible spodumene throughout. Handheld laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) quickly confirmed lithium in selected crystals.The firm believes the location gives the discovery immediate and long-term benefits. Remote mining projects across northern Canada frequently stall under the high cost of building roads and power grids from scratch. Victory sits directly beside the Trans-Canada Highway, with rail lines, electrical transmission, and natural gas pipelines already in place. 2027 drill testsMoreover, finding a third major deposit alongside the Bounty and Last Resort zones improves the property’s prospects as a future raw-material supplier for Rock Tech’s proposed Red Rock processing facility.Still, seasoned mining observers know that surface rock tells only part of the story. Handheld scanner readings and selective grab samples serve strictly as early indicators rather than commercial guarantees. Current visual findings outline the exploration span, but do not prove how deep the mineralization extends, whether separate deposits connect underground, or if the rock holds enough consistent grade to mine profitably. Answers will come in phases. Field crews are still mapping and sampling across the expanded trend, while rock samples await formal chemical assays at Actlabs in Thunder Bay. Those laboratory results will determine true lithium concentrations and dictate where Rock Tech sinks its first drill holes when a planned maiden drill program kicks off in 2027.

title: Nanogenerators turn everyday movement into power for wearable devices
content: Researchers at the University of Surrey have developed a framework that could help wearable devices generate electricity from everyday movements and vibrations, reducing their reliance on batteries. Developed with university spin-out Z-PULSE, the model predicts how much power triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) can produce from mechanical motion. These lightweight, flexible devices generate electricity when two charged surfaces come into contact and separate.The new framework combines mechanical and electrical behavior in a single model, helping engineers understand energy losses and optimize generators to produce more power from irregular vibrations.Vibrations into electricityThe new modeling framework could help engineers design more efficient devices capable of generating electricity from everyday vibrations.The technology focuses on TENGs, lightweight and flexible devices that convert mechanical movement into electrical energy. The framework predicts how mechanical vibrations are converted into useful electrical power, potentially supporting future battery-assisted or battery-independent wearable electronics and autonomous sensors.TENGs generate electricity through a process called contact electrification. When two different materials come into contact, they develop opposing electrical charges. Separating the surfaces creates a potential difference that drives electrical charges through an external circuit, producing electricity. The process is similar to static electricity generated when a balloon is rubbed against a sweater.Unlike conventional electromagnetic generators, TENGs can harvest energy from relatively slow and irregular movements. This makes them attractive for applications involving human motion, structural vibrations, and other low-frequency mechanical energy sources. However, predicting their actual electrical output has remained difficult because conventional circuit models often overlook the mechanical behaviour of the devices.The team addressed this limitation by developing a lumped electromechanical equivalent-circuit (LEEC) framework. The model combines the mechanical and electrical components of a TENG into a single mathematical representation, allowing engineers to examine how energy moves through the complete system.It incorporates parameters such as the device’s mass, spring stiffness, and mechanical damping, alongside electrostatic forces, surface charge density, and the changing distance between the charged materials. It also accounts for the electrical load connected to the generator.By representing mechanical components as their electrical equivalents, the framework allows researchers to use established circuit-analysis techniques to study energy conversion. This helps identify how much mechanical energy is transferred into electrical output and how much is lost through damping and other processes.“A self-powered system becomes much more interesting when its generated signal is not treated only as electricity. The waveform also contains information about the mechanical environment that produced it. This creates the possibility of future devices that can harvest energy from their surroundings while sensing those surroundings at the same time,” said Sajib Roy, a postgraduate research student at the university, in a statement.TENGs sense roadsAn important aspect of the approach is its ability to account for mechanical resonance. This occurs when the frequency of an external vibration approaches a device’s natural frequency, amplifying its movement. The researchers found that matching the operating frequency to this resonance can substantially improve electrical output by increasing the speed and amplitude of movement between the charged surfaces.Experimental tests using TENG devices with different mechanical properties showed close agreement with the model’s predictions. The researchers also examined how changes in oscillating mass, spring stiffness and damping influence resonance and power generation.In experiments involving different surface charge densities, four borophene-modified TENG devices produced progressively higher electrical outputs. The best-performing sample achieved an estimated energy-conversion efficiency of approximately 14.2 percent. The model also predicted a maximum cycle-averaged theoretical efficiency of around 54 percent under the investigated conditions.The researchers demonstrated another potential application by mounting a TENG on a bicycle mudguard to monitor road conditions. Vibrations generated while traveling over smooth, rough, and gravel surfaces produced distinct electrical signals. A classification model used these signals to distinguish among the three road types with 96.7 percent accuracy.The findings demonstrate that TENGs could potentially serve as both energy harvesters and self-powered sensing devices. The framework provides engineers with a way to optimize their mechanical and electrical characteristics together, rather than treating them as separate design problems.

title: Rare US Air Force RC-135U spy plane spotted over the Black Sea
content: A rare U.S. Air Force electronic reconnaissance aircraft, one of only two in the military’s entire inventory, conducted a high-profile surveillance mission over the Black Sea on November 16, 2026. The flight marks a notable return of visible American intelligence-gathering aircraft to a region where European and NATO surveillance platforms have carried the bulk of recent monitoring duties.Operating under the radio callsign JAKE27, the modified Boeing RC-135U Combat Sent, carrying tail number 64-14849, departed from Royal Air Force (RAF) Mildenhall in the United Kingdom before transiting toward southeastern Europe. Once over international airspace in the eastern Black Sea, the aircraft executed multiple racetrack orbits over the basin during an approximately two-hour window before returning toward its British base.Joint NATO surveillance over the coastlineAccording to open-source flight-tracking data logged by aviation monitoring group ItaMilRadar and public ADS-B transponder records, the RC-135U flew alongside a NATO E-3A Sentry airborne early warning and control aircraft (registration LX-N90444, callsign NATO01) departing Geilenkirchen, Germany. While the NATO E-3A patrolled along the western Black Sea coastline to maintain broad aerial and maritime radar coverage, the American RC-135U focused deeper over the eastern basin.The Black Sea mission followed two earlier European sorties by the same airframe after its forward deployment to the United Kingdom earlier in November. Open-source tracking showed the aircraft monitoring Russia’s heavily militarized Kaliningrad exclave on November 13, following an earlier intelligence run along the Finnish-Russian border. The deployment also unfolded amid heightened regional tensions following recent drone strikes on merchant shipping near Romanian waters and elevated alert levels around the Kerch Strait.Inside the Combat Sent’s specialized sensorsUnlike the more numerous RC-135V/W Rivet Joint fleet, which primarily intercepts communications and provides near-real-time tactical intelligence to field commanders, the RC-135U Combat Sent is engineered specifically for technical electronic intelligence (ELINT). Operated by the Air Force’s 55th Wing at Offutt Air Force Base, Nebraska, only two Combat Sent airframes exist, each with distinct structural modifications overseen by L3Harris Technologies.Externally, the four-engine jet is immediately recognizable by large cheek fairings along the forward fuselage, an extended tail cone, and specialized antenna arrays mounted on its chin and wingtips. Inside, a minimum crew of eight electronic warfare officers, known as “Ravens,” and six or more technical specialists operate precision signal-collection receivers. Rather than simply listening to radio chatter, the Combat Sent locates, records, and analyzes the exact operating frequencies, pulse characteristics, and waveforms of foreign land, naval, and airborne radar systems.Why technical radar mapping mattersThe scientific and technical data collected during Combat Sent sorties feeds directly into national defense databases used by electronic warfare engineers. By dissecting how an adversary’s air-defense or coastal radar systems behave under active conditions, defense specialists can identify vulnerabilities, reprogram onboard radar warning receivers, and develop tailored electronic countermeasures for allied fighter and bomber crews.Equipped with aerial refueling capability and a service ceiling of 50,000 feet (15,240 meters), the RC-135U can remain on station for extended periods without entering contested airspace. While U.S. unmanned drones and manned intelligence jets had maintained a lower public profile over the Black Sea in recent weeks, Monday’s sortie signals Washington’s continued focus on mapping evolving electronic threats across NATO’s eastern flank.

title: 人民日报：新型电网，新在哪？-索比光伏网
content:
草原深处的毡房、大漠边缘的村落、大山深处的人家……在曾经远离电网的远方，一盏盏电灯次第亮起，成为我国电力发展的生动注脚。
当前，我国已经建成全球规模最大的电力供应体系。今年前9月，全社会用电量达80734亿千瓦时，同比增长3.9%。
与此同时，我国电力体系也在发生着一系列新变化——
在发电侧，新能源从边缘迈向主力，在我国电力结构中主体地位日益凸显，截至2026年9月底，我国风电和太阳能发电累计装机容量达到20.1亿千瓦。与传统稳定可控的火电相比，新能源“阴晴不定”，给电网带来了波动性和不确定性。
在用电侧，新兴产业持续壮大，2025年我国充换电服务业用电增速达48.8%，八大算力枢纽节点用电量近三年平均增长39.5%，远高于全社会用电量增速。这些产业不仅要求“有电可用”，更需要高品质供电。
高比例接入的新能源和高速增长的新负荷，正在同一张电网上加速交汇。今年4月28日召开的中共中央政治局会议指出，“加强水网、新型电网、算力网、新一代通信网、城市地下管网、物流网等规划建设。”新型电网，被纳入国家顶层设计。
电力供应充足、用电安全可靠，离不开一张强大的电网。如何加快推进新型电网建设?记者进行了采访。
优化完善电网新架构
广州天河，棠下变电站，一场关于电网主网新架构的“大手术”正在加快进行——220千伏天河棠下柔直背靠背工程的施工现场，工人们施工正酣。
工程为何而建?南方电网广东广州供电局项目管理中心柔性直流工程项目部高级经理谢剑翔给记者展示了一张图：珠江穿城，广州电网被分为南北两域，其中给广州中东部供电的三大核心片区里，木棉、增城片区位于珠江以北，广南片区位于珠江以南。
“受珠江天然阻隔，在原有的电网架构下，三个片区运行相对独立，电力互济能力难以满足未来不断增长的用电需求。”广州供电局电力调度控制中心电网规划科高级经理郭挺表示，建设这个工程相当于在三个供电片区之间新建一个智能“能量控制器”。“这个‘控制器’建在棠下——三个供电片区的中心，一旦遇到某个区域缺电，这个装置能在毫秒间把另外两个片区的富余电力及时送过来进行支援。”
据悉，工程投运后，三大片区互济能力预计可达205万千瓦，最高可向天河区核心区域支援供电90万千瓦。
“相较于传统电网，新型电网建设要更加注重系统思维，立足区域资源禀赋、产业结构特征、负荷特性及分布等，与国土空间格局在时间和空间维度上统筹规划，从而实现更大范围跨区域能源资源优化配置。”国网能源研究院能源所能源战略研究室主任闫晓卿表示，电网有主干电网、配电网，还有智能微电网，如同“高速公路—城乡道路—社区支路”的三级路网，要建设好新型电网，优化完善电网新架构是关键，实现主配微有机协同，为能源转型与高质量发展提供稳定电力支撑。
主网要“柔”。作为电网的“大动脉”，负责电能跨区域传输，要适配新能源的波动性特征，强化区域电网互济能力。
配网要“韧”。过去配电网的“单向送电”，现在升级为“双向互动”，面对自然灾害，可以主动自愈来压减停电范围，能靠本地电源和储能把重要负荷稳稳兜住。
微网要“弹”。微电网集成分布式电源、储能、负荷的小型自治系统，在应急保供、绿色工业、智慧村镇场景落地示范，既能并网运行，也能独立运行，可以“自己管好自己”。
主配微架构的升级，是一场正在全国铺开的系统性建设。但考验，也往往在工程之外。
“‘十五五’时期，我国新型电网投资预计将超过5万亿元，新增投产15回特高压直流输电通道，同时还将推动配电网数智化升级改造，加快智能微电网发展。但与此同时，土地资源日益紧张、邻避效应加剧，使得大型项目落地实施存在不少难题。”南方电网公司规划部规划管理处高级经理杨振纲建议，要完善要素协同保障体系，畅通工程落地实施通道。
向内，积极应用紧凑型布置、地下敷设等节地技术，为节约土地空间提供技术支撑。
向外，推动输电廊道布局与国土空间、城乡建设、生态环保等规划深度链接，将关键廊道纳入国土空间规划，为清洁能源的大范围配置创造良好外部条件。
攻坚突破电网新技术
如果说新架构是载体骨架，回答“建什么样的电网”，那么新技术就是支撑手段，回答“靠什么来实现”。
杨振纲认为，电网新技术不是单一设备的简单迭代，而是让电网“柔”“韧”“弹”的整套技术体系。
——装上新型储能，给电网备好“稳定器”。
浙江宁波余姚黄家埠镇，光耀热电厂区北侧，49个白色储能集装箱沿场地铺开，在晨光里连成一片安静的银灰色方阵。海风从杭州湾方向吹来，一排排舱体整齐排列，温控风扇低声运转。这里是朗辰新能源50兆瓦/100兆瓦时独立储能电站，也是宁波建成的首个电网侧独立储能站。
走近舱体，里面的“分工”各有讲究：东侧磷酸铁锂舱容量大，负责削峰填谷;西北侧钛酸锂舱反应快，专门应对电网频率波动：电网一有波动，它能在数十毫秒内完成功率调整，传统火电机组则需要30秒左右。
宁波是全国分布式光伏装机率先破千万千瓦的城市，工厂屋顶、滩涂、田间都成了发电场。但光伏“看天吃饭”，一片云飘过，发电曲线就可能陡然起落。国网宁波供电公司调控专家马旭介绍，从削峰填谷到功率响应，新型储能让波动的绿电既发得出也用得稳，相当于给城市电网备了一块可随时调用的“充电宝”和“稳定器”。
——应用人工智能，化“波动性”为“确定性”。
今年5月下旬，南方电网电力负荷连续4天创新高，最高达2.75亿千瓦，用电高峰较以往提前一个多月到来。
应对这场大考，离不开一个个“智能大脑”。南方电网气象预测人工智能大模型“天象”提前一周准确锁定5月下旬的极端高温态势，并滚动输出温、湿、雨及风速等多维度精细化预报，日前气温预测平均偏差仅0.5摄氏度;“天衍”负荷预测智能体提前14天解锁高温天气下的负荷态势，研判出广东晚峰负荷高企、云南新能源出力大幅减少的供需紧张形势，不仅给出预测大小，还告知预测结果是怎么来的。
“调度部门据此精准调用抽水蓄能、燃气机组和跨省区互济资源，最高释放新型储能电力678万千瓦，相当于一座二线城市的用电规模，有效应对了高温天气用电大考。”中国南方电力调度控制中心技术专家肖亮说。
眼下，预测、仿真、规划、巡检……人工智能正在渗透电网运行的每一个环节。肖亮认为，人工智能是新型电网最重要的技术方向之一，海量新能源与多元新业态的接入，使电网很难按照过去常规方式去调控，必须用好数智技术，将这些海量元素带来的“波动性”转化为“确定性”，优化电网资源配置和保障电力供给安全。
提质升级电网新服务
架构和技术的升级，最终落脚点在服务。
在深圳，有一个没有厂房的“电厂”——虚拟电厂，正在为城市用电提供一种新型的服务。
“作为电力系统新业态，虚拟电厂构建了一个可以灵活调配的资源池，把充电桩、楼宇空调、分布式储能等分散的可调节资源整合起来，与人工智能技术深度融合，参与电网的调控。”深圳虚拟电厂管理中心高级经理李江南介绍，目前，深圳虚拟电厂管理平台已接入61家运营商、1.4万余个用户，汇集实时可调负荷超140万千瓦，容量相当于一座中型火电厂。
今年8月12日，深圳电网负荷创历史新高，面对攀升的用电压力，深圳虚拟电厂管理中心当天组织全深圳范围内的日内精准响应，26家虚拟电厂运营商参与其中，让空调温度调高、充电错峰、储能放电，实际响应最大容量达到11.6万千瓦，在用电尖峰时刻缓解了电网的压力。
“电网真正吃紧的是两件事：一是负荷尖峰，3%的尖峰负荷一年就出现几个小时;二是局部重载，某条线路、某个片区短时间被压满，但是电力增容不一定能全覆盖。而虚拟电厂的作用，是能在尖峰和重载时段把充电桩、空调、储能的负荷降下来，虚实相济，灵活又高效。”李江南说。
“十五五”时期，虚拟电厂、算电协同、绿电直连等典型的电网新服务持续落地过程中仍面临不少挑战。
比如新业态用电挑战。算力、高端制造等新型负荷用能需求差异化、可靠性要求高，充电桩、分布式资源等主体机理、结构各异，协同调度、业务对接、市场履约机制尚不完善，服务标准有待健全。
又如系统安全运行挑战。虚拟电厂等调节主体深度参与系统平衡，多元主体协同管控复杂度提升，安全管控压力日益加大。
如何进一步推动新服务提质升级?杨振纲建议，技术上，要推动电网先进技术装备规模化应用、全环节数智化升级;标准上，要持续完善新要素、新业态的并网技术标准和服务标准，健全承载力评估机制。同时，还要充分考虑新型电力系统和新型电网的建设成本，完善全环节价格机制，实现产业链可持续发展。
新型电网建设是电网新架构、新技术、新服务的深刻变革，必须统筹谋划、系统施策。国家能源局电力司副司长谭洪江表示，下一步，国家能源局将持续加强新型电网建设，优化完善电网新架构，攻坚突破电网新技术，提质升级电网新服务，大力推进重点任务和重大工程落地实施。

title: 山西：2027年新能源竞价问题咨询答复 (第四批、第五批)-索比光伏网
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策 > 正外部性 > 可再生能源优惠 > 机制（电）价
政策分类依据: 山西发改委就增量新能源项目机制电价竞价、存量项目机制电价实施细则作出正式答复，属可再生能源机制电价政策
content:
11月17日，山西省发展和改革委员会答复关于2027年新能源竞价问题咨询 (第四批、第五批)，共涉及4个问题，具体如下：
2027年新能源竞价问题咨询答复 (第四批)
2026年11月13日17:00至2026年11月15日17:00，竞价工作咨询邮箱共收到问题2个。经研究答复如下：
问题1：竞价填资料时候未投产，在审核期间投产还需要提交保函吗?或者说在哪天之前并网投产就不需要提交保函?
答复：资质申报期间按未投产项目申报的，需提交履约保函。
问题2：我们属于非自然人的光伏，24年1月16日已经备案，并且在25年6月1号之前投产了3户，剩下的正在陆续投产。目前我们有行政审批局审批的盖章版明细，那我以前6月之前投产的，算是存量用户还是增量用户?需不需要参与竞价?如果需要参与竞价，那原来的补贴需要重新退回吗?
答复：按照《山西省发展和改革委员会 山西省能源局
国家能源局山西监管办公室关于印发〈存量新能源项目机制电价实施细则(试行)〉的通知》(晋发改规发〔2025〕7号)第十条“核准(备案)文件载明的建设容量大于电力业务许可证载明的机组容量且电力业务许可证载明的机组投产时间为2025年6月1日(不含)以前的，可认定为存量项目，容量按照电力业务许可证载明的累计容量确定;也可由企业自主选择放弃纳入存量项目，在核准文件载明的建设容量全部并网后按增量项目政策执行”相关规定，新能源项目存在2025年6月1日(不含)以前投产的机组，可以认定为存量项目，不需要参与竞价，但需要承诺后续机组不再建设;也可以待后续机组全容量并网后，按增量项目参与竞价;如该项目已经认定为存量项目并开展差价结算，则不再认定为增量项目并参与竞价。
2027年新能源竞价问题咨询答复 (第五批)
2026年11月15日17:00至2026年11月16日17:00，竞价工作咨询邮箱共收到问题2个。经研究答复如下：
问题1：我们是太原方联新能源公司，有个增量未并网项目想参与机制竞价，须提交履约保函。咨询太原当地银行，反馈说他们银行有统一发给电网公司的模板，想请问下，这个保函文档可否接收?
答复：不接收。请按照《山西省发展和改革委员会〈关于2027年增量新能源项目机制电价竞价工作有关事项的通知〉》(晋发改商品发〔2026〕243号)文件中所附模板开立履约保函。
问题2：在山西省2027年竞价中，提交了一个非自然人分布式光伏项目，在报价报量时，在申报机制电价中填写的是220元/兆瓦时，忘记保留小数点后三位了，是否影响竞价?

title: SPIE acquires Polish grid specialist ENPROM
content:
SPIE has signed an agreement to acquire ENPROM Group, a Warsaw based electrical
power construction specialist with more than 900 employees.
ENPROM provides design, engineering, installation, modernisation and maintenance
services for transmission lines and substations. The company works with
transmission and distribution system operators in Poland and Germany, as
well as offshore energy developers.
According to the announcement, ENPROM generated around €170 million in
revenue in 2025 and has established a strong position in Poland’s high-voltage
power infrastructure market.
SPIE said the acquisition strengthens its expertise in substations and
overhead transmission lines while expanding its presence in the electrical
power construction EPC market.
SPIE said the transaction is expected to be accretive to adjusted earnings
per share from the first year of consolidation and will be funded through
existing financial resources.
Lukasz Nowiñski, Managing Director at SPIE in Central Europe said: “This
acquisition is an important step in strengthening our position in critical
energy infrastructure and establishing ourselves as a leading player in
this demanding and fast-growing market.”

title: Searenergy Poland to support commissioning of Baltyk 2 and 3 wind farms
content:
Searenergy Poland to support commissioning of Baltyk 2 and 3 wind farms TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Searenergy Poland to support commissioning of Baltyk 2 and 3 wind farms
Searenergy Poland has been awarded a contract by a joint venture between
Equinor and Polenergia to support the construction of the Baltyk 2 and
Baltyk 3 offshore wind farms.
The projects will comprise 100 offshore wind turbines in the Baltic Sea.
Together, the wind farms will have a combined capacity of 1,440 MW, enough
to power an estimated 2 million Polish households.
Under the contract, Searenergy will carry out the hook-up and commissioning
of the projects' offshore substations. The company will also provide commissioning
support for the wind turbines during the construction phase, including
the deployment of onshore and offshore commissioning personnel.
According to the company, Searenergy will also perform corrective maintenance
on the transition pieces to ensure they are ready for turbine installation.
"We look forward to bringing the full breadth of our group's expertise
to these projects and creating value for the joint venture of Equinor and
Polenergia," said Natalia Kress, managing director of Searenergy Poland.
First power is currently expected in 2027, with full commercial operations
scheduled to begin in 2028.

title: Kishorn floating wind foundation factory plans move forward
content:
Slipform Engineering has announced progress plans for a new factory at
Kishorn that could produce up to 36 concrete floating offshore wind foundations
The proposed Slip4Wind® facility aims to support more than 500MW of offshore
wind capacity annually.
The company plans to use its expertise to manufacture foundations weighing
around 20,000 tonnes each. A specially designed gantry system would move
production equipment around the structures, allowing the foundations to
remain in place during construction.
Once completed, the foundations could be transferred directly into the
water from the manufacturing site. The approach is intended to reduce the
need to move the structures around the facility during production.
Through the Offshore Wind Growth Partnership's SmartStart Manufacturing
Programme, the National Manufacturing Institute Scotland assessed the proposed
factory's production capacity, costs and workforce requirements.
Eamon Hanley, founder and managing director at Slipform Engineering, said:“Our plans for Slip4Wind® at Kishorn are designed to reduce some
of the major costs associated with traditional manufacturing methods, particularly
the need to transport these enormous structures around a site before they
enter the water.”

title: Siemens Gamesa secures turbine deal for 1GW Zeevonk offshore wind farm
content:
Siemens Gamesa has been selected by Vattenfall and Copenhagen Infrastructure
Partners (CIP), through their joint venture Zeevonk, as the turbine supplier
for Phase I of the 1 GW Zeevonk
offshore wind farm.
Under the agreement, Siemens Gamesa will supply 69 offshore wind turbines,
each with a capacity of 15 MW. Each turbine will feature 115 metre long
blades and a rotor diameter of 236 metres.
Some of the turbines will also feature Siemens Gamesa's GreenerTower, which
uses lower-emission steel to help reduce the tower's carbon footprint.
The company will also deploy its RecyclableBlade technology, making it
easier to separate materials for reuse when the blades are decommissioned.
Under a separate agreement, Siemens Gamesa will provide long-term service
and maintenance for the wind farm, including monitoring and operational
support.
"Zeevonk is a large and ambitious project, and selecting Siemens Gamesa
as turbine supplier is an important step toward execution. Strong supplier
partnerships are essential to delivering a competitive offshore wind project
on this scale," said David Flood, head of offshore wind at Vattenfall.
According to Vattenfall, the agreement means all of the project's key suppliers
for the construction phase are now in place.
Felix Pahl, partner at CIP, said: "With the project's two largest
contracts now in place, we are moving decisively toward a final investment
decision and bringing Zeevonk into execution."

title: Ørsted awarded Earthshot Prize in Fix Our Climate Category
content:
Ørsted has won this year's Earthshot Prize in the Fix Our Climate category,
recognising its contribution to the offshore wind industry.
The award recognises the company's transition from oil and gas to offshore
wind, with renewable energy now accounting for 99% of Ørsted's energy production.
Rasmus Errboe, CEO of Ørsted, said: "Twenty years ago, Ørsted was
one of Europe's most fossil fuel-intensive energy companies. We made a
deliberate decision to fundamentally transform our business and help build
offshore wind into a global industry."
Founded by Prince William in 2020, the Earthshot Prize annually chooses
five winners selected from 15 finalists for their contributions to addressing
environmental challenges. According to the
award announcement, Ørsted currently has more than 11 GW of offshore wind
capacity installed globally, with an additional 7.2 GW under construction.
Amanda Dasch, chief development officer at Ørsted, said: "Ørsted's
transformation shows that fundamental change in the energy system is possible
while continuing to invest in and deliver the secure, affordable renewable
electricity that society needs."
The company said it will continue to support the offshore wind sector by
helping make offshore wind more competitive and sustainable while reducing
emissions across the supply chain.

title: Why Anthropic’s IPO Is Making Philanthropist Craig Newmark Hold Back on AI Safety Donations
content: Craigslist founder Craig Newmark says he’s recently become worried about AI’s potential to cause serious harm to critical infrastructure and human society. He’s considered directing some of his philanthropic funding towards organizations trying to make sure powerful AI doesn’t harm humans. But Newmark told me he is holding back for now because he expects a tsunami of donations from newly wealthy Anthropic employees to such organizations, following Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO this week. These potentially outweigh what he could give, and he feels his money could have more utility elsewhere. “Lots of people are paying lots of attention to it, so I can focus in other areas,” Newmark said in a video interview earlier this month. “Now, maybe I'm being naive thinking that the people developing AI will be the most concerned about its safety,” Newmark said. If AI employees don’t donate to such groups, Newmark says he may have to call “very publicly and very loudly” for philanthropic support for AI safety in addition to his own.

title: Microsoft Nears $500 Million Deal to Sell AI to ByteDance, Irking OpenAI
content: ByteDance is in advanced talks to spend an additional roughly $500 million on cloud services from Microsoft, primarily to use OpenAI models from Microsoft’s Azure cloud, according to two people with knowledge of the situation. The move to expand the Chinese firm’s already large contract with Microsoft has drawn the ire of OpenAI. The AI company has complained to Microsoft in recent months that it believes Chinese firms are “distilling” its AI, or running OpenAI models to create their own competing AI models, according to the people with knowledge of the discussions. OpenAI itself prevents most Chinese firms from using its AI, but Microsoft—which has the rights to sell OpenAI’s technology—doesn’t impose the same restrictions.

title: Nvidia’s Board Rebuffs Jensen
content: Well, that was embarrassing. A few hours after Nvidia’s recently departed CEO Jensen Huang issued a plaintive statement saying he’d love his job back, company chair Harvey Jones sent back a message: no chance, buddy. In an unusual appearance on the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Jones stated unequivocally that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also added something the board didn’t say when it announced Huang’s exit last Thursday: that the exit came “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.” So now it’s clear: it was Huang’s affairs (with a subordinate and a business partner) that caused his exit, and not, for instance, concerns about Nvidia’s possible involvement in smuggling of its chips into China.

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
content:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company
billions of dollars
in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an
AI-powered humanoid robot
up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an
AI-assisted cyberattack
You go to the movies and see
Sam Altman
being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a
Grok-fied version of
The Odyssey
. You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
content:
The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
Plus: The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”
Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.
How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?
—Amit Katwala
Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region's two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.
Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.
—Casey Crownhart
MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.
As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

What’s next for IVF
IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that.
Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease.

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
content:
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
Osmo’s smell model is already being used in the fragrance industry. But are medical diagnostics and threat detection a sniff too far?
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”
“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”
In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.
Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.
A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.
Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)
The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.
Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.
But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.
Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.
But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”
In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.
“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

Studierende und Forschende der THWS entwickeln sprachgesteuerte Assistenzplattform für ältere Menschen
Wie kann künstliche Intelligenz (KI) dazu beitragen, Einsamkeit im Alter zu verringern und älteren Menschen den Zugang zu digitalen Angeboten zu erleichtern? Mit dieser Frage beschäftigt sich das Forschungs- und Entwicklungsprojekt „Carebells“ der Technischen Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS). Auf der internationalen Fachkonferenz VapiCon in San Francisco, USA, stellten Prof. Dr. Ulrich Gartzke und Masterstudent Bhuvana Chandra Thota das Projekt einem internationalen Publikum aus KI-Entwicklern, Unternehmen und Forschungseinrichtungen vor.
Carebells ist eine digitale Plattform, die ältere Menschen im Alltag unterstützen, deren soziale Kontakte fördern und die Menschen zu mehr Aktivität und Austausch anregen soll. Im Mittelpunkt steht die sprachgesteuerte KI-Assistentin „Bella“. Mit Bella können Nutzerinnen und Nutzer Gespräche führen, Informationen abrufen, sich an Termine erinnern lassen oder gemeinsam über aktuelle Nachrichten sprechen. Ergänzt wird das Angebot durch Videotelefonie, Bewegungsangebote und weitere alltagspraktische Funktionen.
Einfache Bedienung durch künstliche Intelligenz
Bei der Entwicklung von Carebells wurde besonderer Wert auf die Bedürfnisse älterer Menschen gelegt. Große Bedienelemente, eine übersichtliche Gestaltung und insbesondere die Steuerung durch gesprochene Sprache sollen den Zugang zu digitalen Angeboten erleichtern.
Eine zentrale Rolle spielt dabei die sogenannte „Voice AI“, also künstliche Intelligenz, die gesprochene Sprache verstehen und darauf reagieren kann. Das interdisziplinäre Entwicklungsteam, an dem insbesondere Studierende des Masterstudiengangs Artificial Intelligence und das Center für Künstliche Intelligenz (CAIRO) der THWS beteiligt sind, hat hierfür verschiedene technische Lösungen entwickelt.
So verfügt Bella über eine Erinnerungsfunktion, mit der sie wichtige Informationen aus früheren Gesprächen aufgreifen kann. Erzählt eine Nutzerin beispielsweise von der Einschulung ihrer Enkelin, kann Bella beim nächsten Gespräch danach fragen. Dadurch sollen persönlichere und kontinuierlichere Dialoge entstehen.
Weitere Entwicklungen ermöglichen es, Bewegungs- und Unterhaltungsvideos per Sprache zu steuern oder Informationen aus geprüften Wissensquellen in Gespräche einzubeziehen. Eine besondere Funktion entstand in Kooperation mit der Main-Post: Die regionale Tageszeitung stellt Nachrichtenartikel zur Verfügung, die Bella nicht nur vorlesen, sondern auch als Ausgangspunkt für Gespräche nutzen kann. So können aktuelle Ereignisse Erinnerungen wecken und zum persönlichen Austausch anregen.
Internationale Fachveranstaltung für sprachbasierte KI
Die vom US-amerikanischen Technologieunternehmen Vapi organisierte Konferenz VapiCon zählt zu den großen internationalen Fachveranstaltungen für sprachbasierte künstliche Intelligenz. Laut Veranstalter bringt sie mehr als 1.200 Teilnehmende sowie über 50 Referentinnen und Referenten aus Forschung, Technologieunternehmen und Start-ups zusammen. Auf dem Programm standen unter anderem Beiträge von Fachleuten aus Unternehmen wie OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Deepgram, Twilio und SpaceX. Im Mittelpunkt standen neue Sprachmodelle, die Entwicklung intelligenter Sprachassistenten sowie deren Einsatz in der Praxis.
Carebells wurde im Programmteil „Voice AI in the Wild: Unique Deployments“ präsentiert, in dem innovative praktische Anwendungen sprachbasierter KI vorgestellt wurden. „Die Möglichkeit, unser Projekt auf einer der wichtigsten internationalen Konferenzen für Voice AI vorzustellen, ist eine große Ehre“, erklärt Prof. Dr. Ulrich Gartzke, der das Projekt Carebells an der THWS koordiniert. „Sie zeigt, dass unser Konzept und die von unseren Studierenden mitentwickelten technischen Lösungen auch international auf Interesse stoßen. Die Atmosphäre hier ist großartig. Wir haben viel positives Feedback erhalten, spannende Kontakte geknüpft und zahlreiche Anregungen für die Weiterentwicklung mitgenommen.“
Auch Bhuvana Chandra Thota, Masterstudent im Studiengang Artificial Intelligence und maßgeblich an der technischen Entwicklung von Carebells beteiligt, zeigte sich beeindruckt: „Die Konferenz zeigt, welches enorme Potenzial in sprachbasierter künstlicher Intelligenz steckt. Besonders spannend ist der Austausch mit Entwicklern und Forschenden aus führenden Technologieunternehmen. Wir können unsere eigenen Lösungen vorstellen und gleichzeitig erfahren, wie andere Teams technische Herausforderungen lösen.“
Regionale Zusammenarbeit mit internationaler Perspektive
Carebells wird an der THWS in enger Zusammenarbeit mit Partnern aus der sozialen Praxis entwickelt und erprobt. Die finanzielle Förderung erfolgt durch die Vogel Stiftung Dr. Eckernkamp. Zu den regionalen Kooperationspartnern zählen Einrichtungen des Caritasverbands für die Stadt und den Landkreis Würzburg sowie die Seniorenvertretung Würzburg. Die Main-Post unterstützt das Projekt durch die Bereitstellung von Nachrichtenartikeln.
Die Zusammenarbeit zwischen Studierenden unterschiedlicher Fachrichtungen, Wissenschaft und sozialen Einrichtungen ist ein wesentlicher Bestandteil des Projekts. Rückmeldungen älterer Menschen aus der praktischen Erprobung fließen unmittelbar in die Weiterentwicklung ein. Ursprünglich für Seniorinnen und Senioren in Bayern entwickelt, bietet Carebells nach Einschätzung des Projektteams auch Potenzial für den Einsatz in anderen Regionen und Ländern.
Datenschutz und Ethik als zentrale Entwicklungsaufgaben
Neben den technischen Möglichkeiten stehen Fragen des verantwortungsvollen KI-Einsatzes im Mittelpunkt. Gerade bei älteren Menschen sei es wichtig, die Privatsphäre zu schützen, transparent über den Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz zu informieren und eine einfache, selbstbestimmte Nutzung zu ermöglichen, betont Prof. Dr. Gartzke. „Wir möchten die Chancen dieser Technologie nutzen, ohne ihre Risiken aus dem Blick zu verlieren. Deshalb beschäftigen wir uns intensiv mit ethischen Fragen und dem europäischen Datenschutz. Gleichzeitig prüfen wir, wo wir verstärkt europäische technische Lösungen einsetzen können. Für uns muss sich die Technologie an den Bedürfnissen der Menschen orientieren, nicht umgekehrt.“
Über die THWS
Die Technische Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS) zählt zu den größten Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften in Bayern und steht seit ihrer Gründung im Jahr 1971 für hervorragende Lehre und angewandte Forschung. Mit rund 9.200 Studierenden, einem breit gefächerten Angebot von mehr als 60 Studiengängen sowie zwei Promotionszentren deckt die THWS ein weites Spektrum ab, das von Technik über Wirtschafts- und Sozialwissenschaften sowie Sprache bis hin zu Gestaltung reicht. Die THWS ist nicht nur regional in Franken und Bayern verwurzelt, sondern auch stark international ausgerichtet, was sich in zahlreichen Kooperationen und Austauschprogrammen weltweit und nicht zuletzt in einem vielseitigen englischsprachigen Studienangebot widerspiegelt.

title: Vorurteile abbauen per Instagram? – Potsdamer Studie zeigt Wirkung und Grenzen von Kontakt über soziale Medien
content:
Vorurteile abbauen per Instagram? – Potsdamer Studie zeigt Wirkung und Grenzen von Kontakt über soziale Medien
Ein Forschungsteam der Universität Potsdam hat in einem Feldexperiment untersucht, ob Kontakt über soziale Medien Vorurteile verringern kann. Das Ergebnis: Wer drei Tage lang einem fremden Instagram-Profil folgt, urteilt anschließend milder – und zwar nicht nur über die kontaktierte Gruppe. Die Studie ist erschienen im „Journal of the Association for Information Systems“, einer der weltweit führenden Fachzeitschriften für Wirtschaftsinformatik.
Über soziale Medien wird meist mit Blick auf ihre Schattenseiten gesprochen: Hassrede, Desinformation, Polarisierung. Ob dieselben Plattformen unter bestimmten Bedingungen auch das Gegenteil bewirken könnten, ist bislang kaum untersucht. Genau hier setzt eine neue Studie an, die Georg Voronin und Prof. Dr. Stefan Stieglitz vom Lehrstuhl für Wirtschaftsinformatik und Digitale Transformation der Universität Potsdam gemeinsam mit Prof. Dr. Olga Abramova von der Leuphana Universität Lüneburg und Prof. Dr. Chee-Wee Tan von der Hong Kong Polytechnic University durchgeführt haben.
Die Forschenden gingen der Frage nach, ob sich die sogenannte Kontakthypothese aus der Sozialpsychologie auf digitale Umgebungen übertragen lässt. Diese besagt, dass Begegnungen zwischen Angehörigen unterschiedlicher gesellschaftlicher Gruppen Vorurteile abbauen können. Im echten Leben scheitert solcher Kontakt jedoch oft an praktischen Hürden oder Berührungsängsten.
Drei Tage, ein Feed, ein messbarer Effekt
Für das Experiment legte das Team vier fiktive Instagram-Profile an – zwei mit deutsch klingenden, zwei mit arabisch-türkisch klingenden Namen. 218 deutsche Instagram-Nutzerinnen und -Nutzer folgten jeweils einem zufällig zugewiesenen Profil, das drei Tage lang neutrale Alltagsfotos bpsw. von Hausfassaden oder Parks postete. Anschließend wurden die Teilnehmenden erneut befragt.
Wie sich zeigte, schrieben die Befragten nach dem Kontakt Menschen mit türkischem oder arabischem Hintergrund in Deutschland mehr Wärme und mehr Kompetenz zu. In der Folge sank die Bereitschaft zu ablehnendem Verhalten, während die Bereitschaft zu unterstützendem Verhalten stieg.
Besonders bemerkenswert ist ein zweiter Befund: Die Wirkung übertrug sich auch auf eine Gruppe, die am Kontakt gar nicht beteiligt war. Auch gegenüber LGBTQIA+-Personen ging die Bereitschaft zu ablehnendem Verhalten zurück. Dieser sogenannte Übertragungseffekt ist bislang vor allem aus der Offline-Forschung bekannt; für digitale Kontexte gab es dazu kaum Belege.
„Unsere Daten zeigen deutlich, dass soziale Medien Vorurteile abbauen können. Die spannende Frage ist, warum die Funktionen, die das leisten könnten, bislang kaum genutzt werden“, sagt Georg Voronin.
Was die Studie nicht zeigt
Die Forschenden ordnen ihre Ergebnisse zurückhaltend ein. Die gemessenen Effekte sind klein bis mittel und bewegen sich in einer Größenordnung, wie sie auch für direkten Kontakt berichtet wird. Zudem beruhen die Erkenntnisse auf Einschätzungen in einem Fragebogen und nicht tatsächlichen Handlungen. Auch die langfristige Wirkung über die drei Tage hinaus bleibt offen.
„Unsere Ergebnisse zeigen, dass wir in Debatten, wie bspw. um den Digital Services Act, nicht nur auf die Abwehr von Schattenseiten wie Hassrede und Polarisierung blicken sollten. Plattformen besitzen auch das bisher weitgehend ungenutzte Potenzial, den gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt zu fördern, wenn digitale Räume verantwortungsvoll gestaltet werden“, so Prof. Dr. Stefan Stieglitz.
Die Arbeit entstand u.a. im Projekt CYLENCE (13N16636), das vom Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) gefördert wird.

Voronin, G., Abramova, O., Stieglitz, S., & Tan, C. W. (2026). Social Media-Enabled Intergroup Contact: Evidence of Primary and Spillover Effects from an Intervention Study. Journal of the Association for Information Systems, 27(6), 1402–1446. DOI: https://doi.org/10.17705/1jais.01007

content:
Von der Tech-Branche zum KI-Journalismus

Im Porträt: Nicolas Killian, Alumnus der Tiefgang-Talente der Klaus Tschira Stiftung, berichtet als Tech-Korrespondent der ZEIT aus dem Silicon Valley - Bewerbung jetzt wieder möglich.
Heidelberg/München 18. November 2026. In ihren Alumni-Porträts stellt die Klaus Tschira Stiftung von ihr geförderte Menschen vor, die wichtige Impulse in Wissenschaft, Forschung und Gesellschaft setzen. Heute: Wie wird aus einem Wirtschaftsinformatiker, der selbst an neuen Technologien gearbeitet hat, ein Journalist, der ihre Entwicklung kritisch begleitet? Diesen Weg ist Nicolas Killian gegangen.
Nach seinem Studium der Informatik und Betriebswirtschaft an der Technischen Universität München und in China arbeitete er mehrere Jahre in der Produktentwicklung verschiedener Tech-Start-ups. Dort beschäftigte er sich unter anderem mit Software für selbstfahrende Autos und der Analyse von Batteriespeichern. 2022 entschied er sich für einen Wechsel in den Journalismus und begann seine Ausbildung an der Deutschen Journalistenschule (DJS). 2024 begann Nicolas Killian für das Digitalressort der ZEIT zu arbeiten und seit Februar 2025 berichtet er als KI-Korrespondent aus San Francisco und dem Silicon Valley.
Im Mittelpunkt seiner journalistischen Arbeit stehen Künstliche Intelligenz, die Menschen hinter ihrer Entwicklung und die Frage, wie diese Technologie unsere Gesellschaft verändern könnte.
Während seiner Ausbildung an der Deutschen Journalistenschule wurde Nicolas Killian als „Tiefgang-Talent 2022“ von der Klaus Tschira Stiftung gefördert. Mit dem Förderprogramm unterstützt die Klaus Tschira Stiftung Journalistinnen und Journalisten dabei, sich intensiv mit wissenschaftlichen Themen auseinanderzusetzen und diese verständlich für ein breites Publikum aufzubereiten.
Menschen aus Naturwissenschaft, Technik und Forschung, die sich für einen Einstieg in den Journalismus interessieren, können sich übrigens jetzt schon für den Bewerbungslauf 2027 an der DJS registrieren: Bei der Anmeldung einfach das Häkchen bei „Talentförderung für Naturwissenschaftler“ setzen. Wer dann an der Deutschen Journalistenschule aufgenommen wird, erhält die Unterlagen und kann sich für das Tiefgang-Programm bewerben:
https://djs-online.de/bewerben/
Im Gespräch gibt Nicolas Killian Einblicke in seinen Werdegang, seine journalistische Arbeit und die Erfahrungen, die ihn auf seinem Weg geprägt haben.
Wie würdest du deine Arbeit einem Kind erklären?
Als Journalist spreche ich mit Forschenden, Ingenieurinnen und Ingenieuren, welche neuen Technologien sie gerade entwickeln, warum sie das machen und wie ihre Technologie die Gesellschaft verändern könnte. Am meisten geht es in meiner Arbeit um Künstliche Intelligenz. Denn in den vergangenen Jahren haben Computersysteme “gelernt”, Fragen zu beantworten und zu sprechen. Sie können Menschen, Tiere und andere Dinge auf Bildern erkennen und neue Bilder erschaffen. Sie können Mathe-Aufgaben lösen und programmieren. Diese Künstliche Intelligenz kann also vieles, was auch Menschen können. Manches sogar besser als wir. Viele sind sicher, dass diese Technologie schon bald unser Leben, unsere Ausbildung und unsere Arbeit stark verändern wird. Und an keinem anderen Ort arbeiten so viele Menschen an diesen Computersystemen wie im Silicon Valley, einer Region an der Westküste der USA. Ich bin als Journalist dort hingezogen, um den Menschen hinter dieser Technologie näher zu sein und ihnen Fragen stellen zu können: Wie sicher sind ihre Computersysteme und wie fair sind sie zu den Menschen? Wem helfen sie und wem nicht? Was müssen wir noch lernen? Verlieren Menschen ihre Arbeit, weil ein Computer nun besser darin ist? Und haben ihre Entwickler wirklich die guten Absichten, so wie sie es immer sagen? Was ich lerne, schreibe ich in einem Artikel auf, damit andere verstehen, was gerade passiert und wer die Menschen hinter dieser Technologie sind.
Was verbindet dich mit der Klaus Tschira Stiftung?
Während meiner Zeit an der Deutschen Journalistenschule (DJS) habe ich eine großzügige Förderung von der Klaus Tschira Stiftung bekommen. Der finanzielle Teil war sehr wichtig für das Leben in München. Die Wissenschaftsjournalistinnen und Wissenschaftsjournalisten, die ich für das Mentoring an die Seite bekam, konnten mich bei vielen Fragen unterstützen, zum Beispiel bei der Auswahl meiner Praktika.
Welchen Rat würdest du deinem jüngeren Ich nach dem Schulabschluss geben?
Zuversichtlich, experimentierfreudig und vor allem mutig sein. Nur wenn man Dinge ausprobiert, kann man wissen, ob sie zu einem passen. Auch wenn sie auf den ersten Blick sehr schwierig erscheinen. Journalist werden, zum Beispiel.
Wie sieht ein typischer Tag bei dir derzeit aus?
Meine Arbeitstage bestehen hauptsächlich aus diesen Dingen: Ich lese und recherchiere; ich treffe Menschen und gehe auf Konferenzen, und schreibe Artikel. Je nach Tag überwiegt mal das eine, mal das andere. In San Francisco versuche ich, in die Szene abzutauchen. Denn bei der Entwicklung von KI ist das Silicon Valley der mit Abstand wichtigste Ort der Welt – hier sitzen OpenAI, Anthropic, Google und unzählige Tech-Konzerne, Investoren und Start-ups. Außerdem sind die Universitäten Stanford und Berkeley hier. Die Menschen, die dort arbeiten, besuche ich in ihren Büros, treffe sie im Café und beim Abendessen oder lerne sie auf Veranstaltungen und Partys kennen. Viel unter Leute zu gehen ist wichtig in meinem Job, manchmal brauche ich aber auch Ruhe zum Schreiben.
Wenn man dich an einem freien Sonntag suchen würde: Wo würde man dich wahrscheinlich finden?
Beim Wandern an der Küste nördlich oder südlich von San Francisco. Dort, wo der Pazifik auf die Strände und Klippen Kaliforniens trifft, wo die Pelikane haarscharf übers Wasser gleiten, Seelöwen und ab und an auch Delfine und Wale aus dem wilden Wasser schauen. Perfekt also, um abzuschalten.
Gab es einen Menschen, einen Moment oder einen Impuls, der dein Interesse für Wissenschaft oder deinen heutigen Weg geprägt hat?
Mein Vater hat Luft- und Raumfahrttechnik studiert, später aber Dokumentarfilme gedreht. Von ihm habe ich gelernt, neugierig auf die Welt zu sein. Wahrscheinlich ist das die wichtigste Voraussetzung für Menschen in Wissenschaft und Journalismus – und ganz besonders für Menschen, die beides verbinden.

Der Spritzbeton wurde in der Versuchshalle an der Ruhr-Universität Bochum von einem Roboter aufgetragen.
| Copyright:

Download
Beton besteht größtenteils aus Gesteinskörnung, Wasser und einem Bindemittel, dem Zement. Die Zementherstellung wird für sieben bis acht Prozent des weltweiten CO2-Ausstoßes verantwortlich gemacht. Hauptverursacher ist dabei der im Zement enthaltene Portlandzementklinker. Das Team des Projekts KOINOR-PRO an der Ruhr-Universität Bochum hat einen Spritzbeton mitentwickelt, der ursprünglich als spritzbare Brandschutzbeschichtung für die Ertüchtigung von Tunneln konzipiert wurde. Weil das Material komplett ohne klassischen Portlandzement auskommt, verursacht es wesentlich weniger Treibhausgasemissionen.
Der Einbau daraus gefertigter Bauelemente an einer Bahnstrecke in Kassel ist ein wichtiger Schritt für eine potenzielle Aufnahme in Regelwerke. Spritzbeton kommt zum Beispiel beim Tief- und Tunnelbau als Sicherungsmaßnahme oder zur Sanierung zum Einsatz.
Für die Herstellung des Portlandzementklinkers werden vor allem Kalkstein und Ton bei rund 1.450 Grad Celsius im Drehrohrofen gebrannt. „Für das Brennen des Zementklinkers ist viel Energie notwendig, die aus Verbrennungsprozessen stammt, welche CO2 freisetzen“, erklärt Matthias Rengshausen vom Projekt KOINOR-PRO. Während des Brennens laufen im Material zudem unweigerlich chemische Reaktionen ab, die den Hauptanteil des CO2 bei der Zementherstellung emittieren. „Diese erwünschten Reaktionen dienen dazu, dass der daraus hergestellte Zement später bei Zugabe von Wasser fest werden kann.“
Komplett andere Art der Aktivierung
Wegen der schlechten Klimabilanz wurde der Klinkeranteil in verschiedenen Spritzbetonrezepturen schon reduziert. Ganz weggelassen werden konnte er allerdings noch nicht. Bis jetzt. „Wir haben praktisch bei Null angefangen und setzen auf eine komplett andere Art der Aktivierung des Baustoffs“, erklärt Matthias Rengshausen. Der im Projekt entwickelte Beton besteht überwiegend aus Hüttensandmehl und Flugasche – Nebenprodukten der Stahlproduktion und der Kohleverbrennung. Damit sich der Baustoff verfestigt, wird ein Natriumsilikat-Aktivator beigemischt, der stark alkalisch ist.
„Dieser Aktivator führt dazu, dass sich die Masse durch eine chemische Reaktion sehr schnell verfestigt, was notwendig ist, wenn Beton aufgespritzt wird, beispielsweise auf eine Tunnelwand über Kopf“, sagt Matthias Rengshausen. Damit der Baustoff lange verarbeitbar bleibt und die Schläuche und Pumpen nicht verstopfen, wird der Aktivator erst ganz zum Schluss an der Düse beim Aufspritzen hinzugefügt. „Das hat den Vorteil, dass man die Arbeitsgeräte nicht sofort reinigen muss, wenn prozessbedingt eine Pause entsteht“, erklärt der Forscher.
Labortests belegen gute Materialeigenschaften
Das Projektteam hat seine Rezeptur im Labor getestet und sichergestellt, dass die aufgespritzte Masse an der Wand gut haftet und möglichst wenig davon zurückprallt und auf den Boden fällt. Bei diesen Rückprallverlusten erreicht der neue Beton bisher günstigere – also geringere – Werte als übliche herkömmliche Mischungen. Die Brandfestigkeit und weitere notwendige Materialeigenschaften wurden ausführlich getestet.
„Damit der Baustoff auch tatsächlich in der Praxis eingesetzt werden kann, muss er in die entsprechenden Regelwerke aufgenommen werden“, erklärt Matthias Rengshausen. Dafür muss er zunächst unter realen Bedingungen erprobt werden. Einen wichtigen Schritt in diese Richtung macht der Einbau bei einem Pilotprojekt der Deutschen Bahn. Hier dürfen die Bochumer Forschenden den Teil einer Stützwand beisteuern und diesen Teil über einige Jahre untersuchen und beobachten lassen.
Kooperationspartner
Neben der Ruhr-Universität Bochum sind am Projekt KOINOR-PRO beteiligt: MC Bauchemie, PORR AG, BUNG-PEB Tunnelbau-Ingenieure, DB InfraGO und der STUVA e.V. Das Projekt wird durch das Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt gefördert.
